title: Move curated model-picker metadata to a remotely refreshable catalog with resilient local fallbacks
before: At parent d09ab8ff13329da1715d20e3fb17d47f499fbc18, curated model identifiers and descriptions were compiled into the CLI. OpenRouter selection began from OPENROUTER_MODELS before applying live availability, tool-support, and pricing filters; Nous model and authentication flows read _PROVIDER_MODELS["nous"] directly. Updating either curated list therefore required changing and releasing the CLI, and there was no versioned remote catalog, catalog cache, schema validation, or provider-specific catalog override.
after: At 855366909f659e7f11635dc5bfbd279a1d4ef83e, a versioned JSON manifest published with the documentation site carries curated provider/model metadata. A configurable runtime resolver validates remote manifests, uses fresh disk and in-process caches, refreshes stale data, accepts provider-specific override URLs, and degrades through stale cache to bundled snapshots without raising to picker callers. Existing picker behavior is preserved: OpenRouter still applies live tool-support and pricing filtering to the resolved curated identifiers, while Nous selection and authentication flows consume a helper that always returns either remote or bundled model identifiers.
diff: The commit adds hermes_cli/model_catalog.py for configuration, HTTP retrieval, minimum schema validation, atomic disk caching, TTL handling, overrides, provider-shaped accessors, and cache reset; adds model_catalog defaults to hermes_cli/config.py; adds a published manifest and generator; changes hermes_cli/models.py to resolve remote curation before bundled lists; routes the Nous model and login flows through the new resolver; and adds 21 focused tests covering schema rejection, caching, refresh, failures, stale-cache recovery, disabled operation, overrides, accessors, and bundled-list integration fallbacks. Documentation and sidebar entries describe the contract and operational behavior.

commit.subject: feat(models): remote model catalog manifest for OpenRouter + Nous Portal (#16033)
commit.body_excerpt:
OpenRouter and Nous Portal curated picker lists now resolve via a JSON
manifest served by the docs site, falling back to the in-repo snapshot
when unreachable. Lets us update model lists without shipping a release.

Live URL: https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/api/model-catalog.json
(source at website/static/api/model-catalog.json; auto-deploys via the
existing deploy-site.yml GitHub Pages pipeline on every merge to main).

Schema (v1) carries id + optional description + free-form metadata at
manifest, provider, and model levels. Pricing and context length stay
live-fetched via existing machinery (/v1/models endpoints, models.dev).

Config (new model_catalog section, default enabled):
  model_catalog.url       master manifest URL
  model_catalog.ttl_hours disk cache TTL (default 24h)
  model_catalog.providers.<name>.url   optional per-provider override

Fetch pipeline: in-process cache -> disk cache (fresh < TTL) -> HTTP
fetch -> disk-cache-on-failure fallback -> in-repo snapshot as last
resort. Never raises to callers; at worst returns the bundled list.

Changes:
- website/static/api/model-catalog.json    initial manifest (35 OR + 31 Nous)
- scripts/build_model_catalog.py

evidence_units.claim: The pinned implementation commit states that curated OpenRouter and Nous picker lists now resolve through a hosted JSON manifest, with cache and bundled-list fallbacks so lists can change without a CLI release.

The change adds a schema-versioned manifest with provider blocks, model identifiers, optional descriptions, and free-form metadata, plus a generator that converts the bundled curated lists into that format.
The default configuration enables remote catalog resolution, defines the master URL and 24-hour TTL, and provides a map for per-provider URL overrides.

The catalog loader rejects non-object manifests, missing or unsupported versions, malformed provider blocks, non-list model collections, and model entries without non-empty string identifiers; HTTP, decoding, validation, and I/O failures return no remote manifest instead of escaping to callers.

Catalog resolution uses a fresh disk-backed in-process cache when possible, fetches when forced or stale, writes fetched data through a temporary file and os.replace, returns stale validated disk data after fetch failure, and otherwise returns an empty catalog for higher-level bundled fallback.

Provider resolution optionally fetches a provider-specific manifest first, falls back to the master catalog, and adapts provider blocks into the pre-existing OpenRouter tuple shape or Nous identifier-list shape; empty or unavailable data is represented as None.

OpenRouter now uses remotely resolved tuples when available and otherwise OPENROUTER_MODELS, then retains its existing live availability, tool-capability, pricing, and recommended-model processing. The Nous adapter similarly returns remote identifiers when non-empty and otherwise a copy of the bundled list.

title: Refresh credential-scoped model metadata before starting turns
before: At parent commit 8003609cc703dbf014159055e63a684901855edc, creation of user turns and mailbox-triggered turns did not ask the model manager to reconcile its in-memory catalog with the currently resolved credentials. A shared catalog could therefore retain metadata fetched for another identity, while turn construction consumed bundled or stale capability metadata. The manager interface had no dedicated best-effort operation for this transition.
after: At commit 2b842962883f2e01526b9c64e383cb2375123a5d, the model manager exposes a best-effort credential-change refresh. It resolves lazy credentials before comparing identities, skips static or already-matching catalogs, otherwise reuses a matching cached catalog or fetches online, and bounds authentication plus cache/fetch work with a five-second deadline while retaining existing fallback metadata on failure. User-turn construction and mailbox-triggered wakeups invoke this reconciliation before constructing turn metadata; mailbox wakeups also recheck that their reserved active turn is still current after the asynchronous discovery wait.
diff: The commit modifies five files with 291 insertions and 2 deletions. It adds the refresh contract and implementation to the model-catalog manager, calls it from the user-turn and mailbox-wakeup entry paths, adds a post-refresh mailbox reservation check, expands command-auth coverage to prove lazy credential resolution precedes identity comparison, and adds parameterized integration coverage for successful refresh, discovery failure, and authentication timeout across user and mailbox turn triggers.

commit.subject: Refresh the model catalog before turns after auth changes (#46508)
commit.body_excerpt:
## Why

Credential changes can leave the in-memory model catalog associated with a different identity, causing subsequent turns to use bundled model metadata instead of the active credentials' catalog.

## What changed

- Refresh mismatched catalogs before user turns and mailbox-triggered wakeups, resolving lazy command credentials before comparing identities.
- Reuse a matching cache or fetch models with a five-second deadline covering auth resolution and cache access. Preserve fallback behavior on failure or timeout; static catalogs need no refresh.
- Recheck the active turn after discovery so an interrupted wakeup does not continue starting a turn.

## Testing

Add coverage for user and mailbox turns after credential rotation, including switching back after another identity replaces the shared catalog. Verify refreshed context windows and request behavior, fallback on discovery failure or auth timeout, and command-auth token rotation.

GitOrigin-RevId: 7e4ad25f1c4476e2023225731924af28c1181767

commit.subject: fix(core): add kimi-k3 token limits (1M context, 128K output) (#7144)
commit.body_excerpt:
Kimi K3 exposes a 1M-token context window and defaults max output to
128K. Without explicit rules it fell through to the generic Kimi
fallback (256K context) and the default output limit, which would
trigger context compaction far too early and under-size the output
budget. Register explicit context-window and output rules so token
accounting matches the model, and mirror them into the
vscode-ide-companion token-limit table.

Docs: https://platform.kimi.com/docs/api/models-overview

title: Keep dynamically discovered provider error registries catchable
before: At first parent 1354e0bfa4847c1a71b9eea7374847a786d81c1b, the provider-error registry treated every exported name ending in "Error" as an exception and explicitly registered litellm.ErrorEventError. ErrorEventError was an ordinary class rather than a BaseException subclass, so the generated tuple could contain a non-catchable class. Runtime handlers using that tuple in an except clause could consequently raise TypeError instead of handling the provider exception.
after: At merge commit fb05748ace65bea780e0766b14b0904fbaac5f7f, discovery considers an "Error" export only when its object is a BaseException subclass, and the known non-exception ErrorEventError entry is removed from the configured registry. The tuple consumed by retry and reporting handlers therefore excludes that invalid member while retaining the configured provider exception classes.
diff: The change modifies aider/exceptions.py in two inseparable parts: it removes ExInfo("ErrorEventError", True, None) from EXCEPTIONS and strengthens the dynamic discovery predicate from a name-suffix check to `var.endswith("Error") and issubclass(getattr(litellm, var), BaseException)`. No test file changed. Existing tests construct the registry, inspect its tuple, and exercise a RateLimitError through a call site whose except clause consumes that tuple.

candidate_atomics.name: normalize-discovered-error-types-by-catchability
candidate_atomics.title: Keep only catchable types in a dynamic error registry
candidate_atomics.description: Reconcile name-based provider error discovery and explicit metadata so the tuple supplied to language-level exception handlers contains only BaseException subclasses. The discovery guard and removal of the known invalid configured member form one operation because either change alone leaves a failure mode: filtering discovery alone does not remove an explicitly configured ordinary class, while pruning only the known class leaves future suffix-matching ordinary classes misclassified.

semantic_action.intent: Prevent provider request handlers from failing with a catch-clause TypeError caused by ordinary classes being included in a dynamically assembled exception tuple.
semantic_action.module_role: provider exception classification and retry-metadata registry
semantic_action.pre_state: Provider exports are classified by an error-like name alone, and at least one configured registry member is an ordinary class that cannot legally participate in an except tuple.
semantic_action.post_state: Discovered error-like exports must inherit from BaseException, and known ordinary classes are absent from the configured registry, so the produced handler tuple contains the intended catchable provider error types.
semantic_action.validation: Construct the registry, assert every emitted tuple member is a class derived from BaseException and the known ordinary error-like export is absent, then raise a later-listed provider exception through a real consumer's except tuple and verify metadata-driven handling occurs without TypeError. The checkout contains construction/tuple tests and a RateLimitError retry-path test, but no new explicit all-members-catchable assertion.
parameters: provider_module: runtime module whose exports are inspected
name_predicate: convention identifying candidate error exports
exception_base: BaseException or the language/runtime catchability root

workflow_graph.goal: Ensure a dynamically assembled provider exception registry can be safely used by retry and reporting handlers without changing their existing error-specific policies.
when_to_use: A runtime error reports that a class in an except clause does not inherit from the language's exception base.
A provider module exposes ordinary classes whose names satisfy the adapter's error-name convention.
An adapter constructs a catch tuple by combining provider-module discovery with an explicit metadata registry.
anti_goals: Do not classify an export as an exception solely because its name ends with an error-like suffix.
Do not add retry metadata for an ordinary provider payload or event class merely to satisfy a discovery-list consistency check.

Do not normalize provider error message or payload contents; this episode concerns exception-type classification and catchability.
not_applicable_when: The provider adapter receives only serialized error payloads and never constructs a language-level exception tuple.
All candidate registry values are already statically guaranteed to inherit from the runtime exception base.
The failure is caused by malformed provider payload fields rather than a non-catchable class in an exception registry.

The current explicit exception metadata registry
The runtime exception base class and catch semantics
Call sites that consume the generated exception tuple
Registry and request-path tests capable of exercising exception handling

title: Reject runtime wrapper instances as provider error bodies
before: At parent commit 66cd061ab468aeae9fd2e38715d3931f7f77f569, provider error normalization treated every non-null object with enumerable keys as a usable body. Node-style streams with a pipe method were excluded, but class instances and wrapper objects without pipe were JSON-serialized. Downstream formatting could then select serialized implementation internals instead of the diagnostic Error.message.
after: At commit 4523528b21c66084fdece7ed3ffa10888bc5ac60, object-valued body candidates are accepted only when non-empty and their prototype is Object.prototype or null. Class instances and response wrappers are rejected, leaving body undefined so downstream formatting preserves Error.message; strings and plain parsed JSON objects remain supported.
diff: The change replaced isNonEmptyObject with isPlainNonEmptyObject for both the nested error field and response-body field. The new predicate checks value type, null, prototype identity, and enumerable-key count. Three regression tests cover rejection of a response-body class instance, rejection of a nested-error class instance, and continued serialization of a plain parsed JSON object. No provider call sites or formatter branches were changed.

commit.subject: fix(ai): treat only plain objects as provider error bodies (#7205)
commit.body_excerpt:
pickBodyText serialized any non-empty object into the error body. SDK error
fields can hold class instances instead of parsed bodies - AWS SDK v3's
$response.body is an HTTP stream/response wrapper - and stringifying one
produced garbage like {"_events":...} as the body, which then replaced
error.message in the composed display string. error.message is where the SDK
puts the real deserialized exception text ("Input is too long...", schema
validation details), so the one useful string was discarded for noise.

The existing pipe-based stream sniffing only covers node-style streams; web
ReadableStreams (pipeTo/pipeThrough, no pipe) and non-stream wrapper classes
slipped through. Require Object.prototype/null prototype before serializing
a candidate body - parsed JSON bodies are plain objects by construction, so
real gateway bodies still surface.

episode.before: At parent commit 66cd061ab468aeae9fd2e38715d3931f7f77f569, provider error normalization treated every non-null object with enumerable keys as a usable body. Node-style streams with a pipe method were excluded, but class instances and wrapper objects without pipe were JSON-serialized. Downstream formatting could then select serialized implementation internals instead of the diagnostic Error.message.
episode.after: At commit 4523528b21c66084fdece7ed3ffa10888bc5ac60, object-valued body candidates are accepted only when non-empty and their prototype is Object.prototype or null. Class instances and response wrappers are rejected, leaving body undefined so downstream formatting preserves Error.message; strings and plain parsed JSON objects remain supported.
episode.diff: The change replaced isNonEmptyObject with isPlainNonEmptyObject for both the nested error field and response-body field. The new predicate checks value type, null, prototype identity, and enumerable-key count. Three regression tests cover rejection of a response-body class instance, rejection of a nested-error class instance, and continued serialization of a plain parsed JSON object. No provider call sites or formatter branches were changed.

evidence_units.claim: The pinned implementation commit is 4523528b21c66084fdece7ed3ffa10888bc5ac60, its parent is 66cd061ab468aeae9fd2e38715d3931f7f77f569, and it changes the shared error-body utility plus its unit test.
evidence_units.source: git show --format=fuller --stat 4523528b21c66084fdece7ed3ffa10888bc5ac60; issue-bundle.json resolved_commit, parent_commit, and changed_files_name_status

evidence_units.claim: The parent implementation serialized any non-null, non-empty object found in error.error or error.$response.body, except response bodies recognized by the separate pipe-method stream check.
evidence_units.source: git show 66cd061ab468aeae9fd2e38715d3931f7f77f569:packages/ai/src/utils/error-body.ts, pickBodyText, isReadableStreamLike, and isNonEmptyObject

evidence_units.claim: The pinned change replaces both generic non-empty-object checks with a plain-object predicate that accepts only Object.prototype or null prototypes and still requires at least one enumerable key.
After the change, string bodies remain directly usable, pipe-like response streams remain excluded, class-instance object bodies are rejected, and non-empty plain objects remain JSON-serialized.
The normalized result controls displayed provider failures: the shared formatter uses Error.message whenever no accepted body exists, while otherwise it may format status and body.
The Bedrock error adapter explicitly chooses normalized status and body only when messageCarriesBody is false and both values exist; otherwise it uses the normalized message.

At the pinned ref, the shared normalizer or formatter is used by Bedrock, OpenAI-compatible, Azure OpenAI, Google, and image-provider error paths, so the classification boundary is shared across multiple adapters.

Do not infer body legitimacy from serializability or enumerable keys alone.
not_applicable_when: The candidate payload is already governed by a reliable typed or schema-validated body contract.
The error corruption occurs after normalization and is unrelated to selecting an object-valued body.

title: Add bounded provider error details to failed API-call diagnostics
before: At parent commit 45f57c2012b05879339d3a79433b1ca2ed94ff5a, the shared API-call exception handler printed the exception type, provider, model, endpoint, and a cleaned 150-character exception message. Although it already extracted api_error.status_code for recovery decisions, the diagnostic header did not display that status, and it never displayed api_error.body, so request-specific provider explanations could be hidden.
after: At commit 712cebc40f2e156036e55ca313f12fda82e35bff, the shared exception handler appends a truthy status code to the failure header as `[HTTP <status>]`. For HTTP 400 only, it also reads the exception body, converts a nonempty body to text, truncates it to 300 characters, and prints it as a separate Details line. Existing retry, fallback, compression, interruption, and client-error classification behavior remains outside the changed block.
diff: The implementation modifies only run_agent.py with seven insertions and one replacement: it derives a conditional status suffix for the existing failure header and adds a guarded HTTP-400 body-display branch after the cleaned error line. No test file changed, and `git diff --check` reports no whitespace errors.

commit.subject: fix(logging): show HTTP status code and 400 body in API error output (#3096)
commit.body_excerpt:
When an API call fails, the terminal output now includes the HTTP status
code in the header line and, for 400 errors, the response body from the
provider (truncated to 300 chars). Makes it much easier to diagnose
issues like invalid model names or malformed requests that were
previously hidden behind generic error messages.

Salvaged from PR #2646 by Mibayy. Fixes #2644.

episode.title: Normalize byte-encoded API error response bodies as UTF-8 without altering unrecognized payloads
episode.before: At parent 96cc8a0daddd1e66597ff862be20434a5d6a1b1b, the error adapter only handled response.data when it was a comma-containing string. It converted every numeric-looking element with String.fromCharCode, so it did not handle Uint8Array/Buffer payloads, interpreted UTF-8 bytes as independent UTF-16 code units, and accepted numeric values outside the byte range. Non-comma strings and strings containing non-numeric elements were left unchanged.
episode.after: At 69bf2d75efda831957172668d0b7e50c14fc0214, the adapter recognizes raw Uint8Array values (including Buffer subclasses) and valid comma-separated integer byte strings, decodes both through TextDecoder as UTF-8, and mutates response.data before API-error logging and rethrow. Comma-separated strings are normalized only when every value is an integer from 0 through 255; ordinary strings, non-numeric sequences, and out-of-range sequences remain unchanged.
episode.diff: The change replaces String.fromCharCode conversion with byte-oriented UTF-8 decoding, adds a direct Uint8Array branch, and adds integer/range validation before constructing a Uint8Array from serialized bytes. Existing normalization call sites remain in the non-streaming request rejection path and the streaming-request setup rejection path. Tests add coverage for raw Uint8Array data, two-byte and three-byte UTF-8 text, and out-of-range preservation while retaining prior ASCII, ordinary-string, and malformed-string cases.

evidence_units.claim: Commit 69bf2d75efda831957172668d0b7e50c14fc0214 is a single-parent implementation commit for PR/issue 23341 and changes the error adapter plus its tests.

The parent implementation only examines comma-containing strings, maps their elements with Number, accepts them when none is NaN, and converts them with String.fromCharCode; it has no raw Uint8Array branch or byte-range check.
The implementation adds direct Uint8Array decoding, validates serialized values as integers in the inclusive 0-255 range, and decodes the resulting bytes using TextDecoder.

The resulting adapter navigates only object-shaped errors with a response.data field; Uint8Array data is decoded directly, while comma-separated strings are decoded only after every parsed element satisfies the byte-domain predicate.
When a non-streaming content request rejects, normalization runs before API-error logging and the same error object is then rethrown.
When creation of a streaming request rejects before returning an async generator, normalization likewise runs before logging and rethrow.
A rejected request carrying response.data as Uint8Array([72,101,108,108,111]) is asserted to rethrow with response.data normalized to "Hello".
Serialized byte strings are asserted to decode multi-byte UTF-8 correctly for both "Héllo" and the three-byte-per-character text "こんにちは".
A serialized sequence containing 256 is asserted to remain unchanged rather than being coerced into a byte array.
Regression cases assert that ASCII serialized bytes still decode to "Hello", an ordinary error message remains unchanged, and a sequence containing a non-numeric element remains unchanged.

The added tests exercise the public generateContent rejection path and inspect the rethrown error object's response.data, providing an oracle for both successful normalization and preservation behavior; the available checkout has all tracked files deleted from the working tree, so this extraction did not execute the test suite.

Normal shutdown and stop paths call unregisterSignalHandlers, which executes and clears all recorded cleanup callbacks, including removal of the new uncaughtException listener.

when_to_use: A long-running interactive process enables raw input, hides the cursor, or enables terminal protocols that ordinary process termination will not reliably restore.

title: Isolate stdio child-process diagnostics from the interactive terminal
before: At parent commit 7db2703b332bbe8afe2c89b1fed2dd8c03cbd9af, the stdio server lifecycle invoked stdio_client(server_params) without an errlog argument. after: At commit 379b2273d95566e8a69eadabceabc6ee08521b49, the process lazily opens and reuses a thread-safe, append-mode, line-buffered diagnostic file with a real file descriptor; falls back first to the null device and finally to parent stderr; writes a best-effort timestamped server-start marker; and supplies the resulting handle as errlog whenever a stdio server is spawned. diff: The implementation modifies only tools/mcp_tool.py: it adds sys and datetime imports, a locked process-wide stderr-handle cache, diagnostic-sink creation and fallback logic, a timestamped header writer, and changes the single stdio_client call from stdio_client(server_params) to stdio_client(server_params, errlog=_errlog) after obtaining the shared sink. The commit reports 81 insertions and 1 deletion; no test file changed.

commit.subject: fix(mcp): route stdio subprocess stderr to log file, not user TTY (#14901)
commit.body_excerpt:
MCP stdio servers' stderr was being dumped directly onto the user's
terminal during hermes launch. Servers like FastMCP-based ones print a
large ASCII banner at startup; slack-mcp-server emits JSON logs; etc.
With prompt_toolkit / Rich rendering the TUI concurrently, these
unsolicited writes corrupt the terminal state — hanging the session
~80% of the time for one user with Google Ads Tools + slack-mcp
configured, forcing Ctrl+C and restart loops.

Root cause: `stdio_client(server_params)` in tools/mcp_tool.py was
called without `errlog=`, and the SDK's default is `sys.stderr` —
i.e. the real parent-process stderr, which is the TTY.

Fix: open a shared, append-mode log at $HERMES_HOME/logs/mcp-stderr.log
(created once per process, line-buffered, real fd required by asyncio's
subprocess machinery) and pass it as `errlog` to every stdio_client.
Each server's spawn writes a timestamped header so the shared log stays
readable when multiple servers are running. Falls back to /dev/null if
the log file cannot be opened.

Verified by E2E spawning a subprocess with the log fd as its stderr:
banner lines land in the log file, nothing reaches the calling TTY.

commit.subject: [codex] Handle Ctrl-C for non-TTY unified exec (#26734)
commit.body_excerpt:
## Why

A long-running unified exec process started with `tty: false` could not
be interrupted via `write_stdin`: ordinary non-TTY stdin writes are
rejected once stdin is closed, but an exact U+0003 payload should still
map to a process interrupt. The interrupt should flow through the same
process lifecycle path as a real signal so Codex preserves
process-reported output and exit metadata instead of fabricating a
Ctrl-C exit code or tearing down the session early.

## What Changed

- Add `process/signal` to exec-server with `ProcessSignal::Interrupt`
and an empty response.
- Add a non-consuming `ProcessHandle::signal` path for spawned
processes; on Unix it sends SIGINT to the process group and leaves
terminate/hard-kill unchanged.
- Route non-TTY U+0003 `write_stdin` through `process.signal(...)`
instead of `terminate`, then let the normal post-write collection path
drain output and observe exit.
- Add exec-server coverage where a shell `trap INT` handler prints the
signal and exits with its own code.
- Add unified exec coverage where a `tty: false` process traps SIGINT,
emits output, and exits with its own code.

## Validation

- `just test -p codex-exec-server
exec_process_signal

evidence_units.claim: Commit f2969f36 has parent f574946960 and states that non-TTY unified-exec processes could not be interrupted through write_stdin; the intended resolution is a real signal path that preserves process-reported output and exit metadata.

In the parent, write_stdin returned StdinClosed for every non-empty non-TTY input. The change defines exact U+0003 as INTERRUPT, invokes process.interrupt only for that exact payload, continues rejecting all other non-TTY input, and then proceeds through the existing output collection and state-refresh path.

UnifiedExecProcess gains an async interrupt operation that adapts the same semantic interrupt to either the direct spawned-process handle or the exec-server-backed process handle without invoking terminate, closing output, cancelling collection, or aborting helper tasks.
The exec-server contract adds typed ProcessSignal::Interrupt, SignalParams, an empty SignalResponse, and the process/signal method.

Signal requests are carried through the exec-server client/session, ExecProcess interface, remote implementation, RPC router and handler, process handler, and local process implementation, so local and remote execution share the same lifecycle operation.

title: Synchronize native PTY exit with public lifecycle completion and make finalization resilient
before: At parent 09e048fd61bc56df18676211f65703e7f0075f3a, PTY execution completed only from the public pty.onExit callback. On Windows ConPTY, native process termination could occur without that callback when the data pipe remained open, leaving the execution result unresolved and the PTY reported active. A resize requested before the first data event could also remain deferred inside the PTY implementation and throw after native process exit. In addition, exceptions from output listeners could reject the serialized processing chain or interrupt final rendering and exit notification, preventing cleanup and result completion.
after: At 4577750da8e9fcee42297a2f54fbae18c0fa6324, the service observes the Windows PTY agent's native exit callback and exit-code state, schedules a 150 ms drain window, and invokes the same idempotent exit handler if the public exit event is lost. It suppresses only post-exit resize operations and the PTY library's specific already-exited resize error. Output emission, processing-chain rejection, final rendering, and exit-listener failures are contained so cleanup and result completion continue. Active PTY state is removed during finalization and activity/resize checks consult ownership and native-exit state.
diff: The commit modifies packages/core/src/services/shellExecutionService.ts and its tests. It introduces a typed internal Windows-agent adapter; wraps agent resize; extracts an idempotent handlePtyExit path shared by public and native exit signals; adds a resettable 150 ms native-exit fallback; makes output and finalization callbacks exception-tolerant; treats rejected output processing as drained for finalization; removes active ownership before asynchronous log cleanup; and tightens activity and resize checks. Three regression tests cover a missing public exit event, a deferred post-exit resize, and an output-listener exception during shutdown.

candidate_workflows.name: harden-pty-exit-and-finalization-lifecycle
candidate_workflows.title: Make PTY termination deterministic across asynchronous exit and output paths
candidate_workflows.description: A partial-order resolution workflow for PTY integrations where native process exit, public exit delivery, deferred control operations, and output callbacks can become desynchronized.

workflow_graph.goal: Ensure that a natively terminated PTY process reaches exactly one completed lifecycle state after bounded output draining, without deferred resize or output-consumer failures preventing cleanup.
when_to_use: A PTY-backed subprocess can terminate at the operating-system layer without reliably producing the library's public exit event.
Control operations may be queued internally and execute after process termination.
Output or lifecycle event consumers are outside the lifecycle owner's trust boundary and may throw during output processing or shutdown.
anti_goals: Do not immediately finalize at the native exit signal when a short bounded window is needed to drain trailing PTY output.

Do not suppress arbitrary resize, rendering, or consumer errors indiscriminately; contain only errors whose failure must not block lifecycle completion, and preserve logging or rethrow unrelated control errors.
Do not create separate cleanup implementations for native and public exit signals.
Do not change command semantics, output formatting, or successful interactive behavior beyond lifecycle hardening.
not_applicable_when: The subprocess API provides one authoritative exit signal that is guaranteed to fire only after output has drained and no lower-level termination signal is available or needed.
No PTY, deferred control-operation queue, or asynchronous output-finalization pipeline is involved.
The desired behavior is to keep a process logically active after confirmed native termination.
inputs: PTY process handle and public exit subscription
native process-exit signal or queryable exit state
execution identifier and active-resource registry
serialized output-processing chain
output/render/exit consumers
bounded output-drain duration
PTY control operations that may be deferred
workflow_graph.entry_state: A PTY execution is registered as active; output and control callbacks may still be pending; public exit delivery is not sufficient to prove timely native termination completion.
workflow_graph.exit_state: Native or public exit has selected one idempotent finalization path; trailing output received during the bounded window has been processed as far as possible; listener failures cannot block cleanup; PTY ownership is removed; and the execution result is resolved with exit metadata.

steps.condition: The PTY implementation can defer resize or another control operation beyond the initiating call.
steps.validation: A control operation queued before readiness executes after native exit without throwing, while unrelated errors are not silently swallowed.

steps.condition: Output, rendering, or exit consumers can throw or reject independently of process state.
steps.validation: An injected output-consumer exception does not prevent the public exit path from resolving the execution result.

steps.condition: A native exit signal or already-populated native exit code is observable before reliable public exit completion.
steps.validation: With the public exit event withheld, native exit resolves the result after the drain window, records the exit code, and clears active state.

validation_ladder: Unit-test the post-exit control-operation guard by flushing a previously deferred resize after native termination.
Unit-test ordinary public-exit finalization with a throwing output consumer and a bounded completion timeout.
Unit-test the missing-public-exit scenario using the native exit signal, the complete drain interval, result metadata, and active-resource state.
Confirm both native and public exit signals converge on one idempotent finalizer so duplicate completion and cleanup are prevented.
stop_conditions: Stop if there is no trustworthy native termination signal or exit state to reconcile with the public lifecycle.
Stop if no bounded drain policy can be justified; an unbounded wait recreates the hang, while immediate cleanup may discard output.
Stop if the proposed interception requires swallowing unrelated operational errors or bypassing the normal shared cleanup path.
Stop and defer promotion if the regression tests cannot establish result resolution and resource-state cleanup.
unresolved_or_deferred: The evidence bundle does not include PR discussion, review rationale, or CI/status-check results.

The regression tests are present as direct validation oracles, but this extraction did not establish an independent local test-run result because the supplied working tree has its tracked files removed; evidence was inspected from the pinned Git objects.
The 150 ms drain duration is repository-specific evidence and should remain a configurable parameter rather than a universal constant.

What measurements or PTY-library guarantees motivated the specific 150 ms drain interval? The implementation and tests establish the value used, but not a cross-project timing rule.
The commit comment and test describe a Windows ConPTY-specific lost-exit mechanism; applicability to other PTY implementations requires independent evidence.

title: Resolve read-only path patterns against the repository root
before: At first parent 9edf9b4186ea08e2fb98897697e4f9b62836bb6f, the read-only command expanded every input with glob.glob(expanded_pattern, recursive=True), so relative pattern discovery used the process current working directory. The discovered path was subsequently passed to coder.abs_root_path(), which joins relative paths to coder.root. After the process changed into a repository subdirectory, a repository-root-relative input such as subdir/test_read_only_file.txt was searched beneath that subdirectory and produced no match, even though later path normalization treated the same input as repository-root-relative.
after: At b911ceaa6125bbb8e11fe741dab10bbf9731bf12, the read-only command calls glob.glob(expanded_pattern, recursive=True, root_dir=self.coder.root). Relative patterns are therefore discovered from the same repository-root base used by coder.abs_root_path(), independent of the process current working directory. Absolute and tilde-expanded inputs remain supported. A regression test changes into a repository subdirectory, adds a file using its repository-root-relative name, confirms that its absolute path enters the read-only set, drops it using the same name, and confirms removal.
diff: The merge changes one implementation line in aider/commands.py by supplying coder.root as glob's root_dir, aligning relative-pattern discovery with downstream repository-root path resolution. It adds a 37-line regression test in tests/basic/test_commands.py covering the non-root-working-directory scenario and the add/drop lifecycle. The focused test could not be executed in the available environment because the system Python lacked pytest and the discovered pytest environment lacked GitPython; git diff --check reported no patch whitespace errors.

episode.title: Resolve read-only path patterns against the repository root
episode.before: At first parent 9edf9b4186ea08e2fb98897697e4f9b62836bb6f, the read-only command expanded every input with glob.glob(expanded_pattern, recursive=True), so relative pattern discovery used the process current working directory. The discovered path was subsequently passed to coder.abs_root_path(), which joins relative paths to coder.root. After the process changed into a repository subdirectory, a repository-root-relative input such as subdir/test_read_only_file.txt was searched beneath that subdirectory and produced no match, even though later path normalization treated the same input as repository-root-relative.
episode.after: At b911ceaa6125bbb8e11fe741dab10bbf9731bf12, the read-only command calls glob.glob(expanded_pattern, recursive=True, root_dir=self.coder.root). Relative patterns are therefore discovered from the same repository-root base used by coder.abs_root_path(), independent of the process current working directory. Absolute and tilde-expanded inputs remain supported. A regression test changes into a repository subdirectory, adds a file using its repository-root-relative name, confirms that its absolute path enters the read-only set, drops it using the same name, and confirms removal.
episode.diff: The merge changes one implementation line in aider/commands.py by supplying coder.root as glob's root_dir, aligning relative-pattern discovery with downstream repository-root path resolution. It adds a 37-line regression test in tests/basic/test_commands.py covering the non-root-working-directory scenario and the add/drop lifecycle. The focused test could not be executed in the available environment because the system Python lacked pytest and the discovered pytest environment lacked GitPython; git diff --check reported no patch whitespace errors.

evidence_units.claim: The pinned merge commit is b911ceaa6125bbb8e11fe741dab10bbf9731bf12, has first parent 9edf9b4186ea08e2fb98897697e4f9b62836bb6f and second parent ba9fdaa755c82994d7aff7404d689d6c721ab283, and identifies PR 2126 as fixing an inability to use the read-only command from another working directory.
In the first parent, cmd_read_only expands user input and invokes glob.glob(expanded_pattern, recursive=True), leaving relative-pattern lookup dependent on the process current working directory.
The implementation adds root_dir=self.coder.root to the glob invocation and makes no other production-code change in the first-parent diff.
After globbing, cmd_read_only passes each returned path to coder.abs_root_path before checking whether it is a file or directory and adding it to the read-only collection.
coder.abs_root_path constructs Path(self.root) / path and converts it to a safe absolute path, establishing the repository root as the downstream base for relative paths.

The added regression test creates a file under a repository subdirectory, changes the process current directory into that subdirectory, invokes cmd_read_only with a repository-root-relative path, and asserts by os.path.samefile that the file is present in coder.abs_read_only_fnames.
The same regression test invokes cmd_drop with the repository-root-relative name and asserts that the file is no longer present in coder.abs_read_only_fnames.

An adjacent pre-existing test supplies an absolute temporary-file path to cmd_read_only and verifies that the external file is added, providing coverage for the absolute-path behavior that the root-base correction must preserve.

title: Harden dangerous-command approval boundaries and preserve explicit bypass semantics
before: At parent 3ab7e2aa9190c32abd8f854f9f6a88ad9a2c3d0e, both dangerous-command entry points reread HERMES_YOLO_MODE from mutable process environment state on every invocation, so in-process code could enable the process-wide bypass after startup. Smart approval accepted any normalized LLM response containing APPROVE or DENY as a substring. Remote-content detection only recognized curl/wget pipelines whose shell token was directly sh or bash. Dangerous commands automatically allowed outside interactive and gateway contexts produced no audit warning.
after: At 4cb3eb03c750c902919906733b79220588ca5f16, process-wide YOLO configuration is parsed once at module import and both approval entry points consult the frozen value while retaining session-scoped bypass and existing hardline guards. Smart approval grants or denies only for exact normalized APPROVE or DENY tokens and escalates every other response. Remote-content detection additionally recognizes path-qualified sh/bash and bash -c forms. The legacy non-interactive, non-gateway auto-approval behavior remains, but each such approval emits a warning containing the matched description and a command prefix. YOLO tests patch the captured configuration value directly and continue checking bypass behavior in both approval entry points.
diff: The commit modifies tools/approval.py and tests/tools/test_yolo_mode.py (20 insertions, 10 deletions). It adds one import-time boolean, replaces two runtime environment checks, tightens two LLM-response comparisons, broadens one dangerous-command regex, adds one warning before a legacy auto-approval return, and updates three tests to patch the module-level captured value instead of mutating HERMES_YOLO_MODE.

commit.subject: fix(approval): harden YOLO bypass, LLM parsing, auto-approve audit, pipe pattern (#23835)
commit.body_excerpt:
* fix(approval): harden YOLO bypass, LLM parsing, auto-approve audit, pipe pattern

- BUG-009 (CRITICAL): freeze HERMES_YOLO_MODE at module import via
  _YOLO_MODE_FROZEN; prevents skills/prompt-injection from calling
  os.environ["HERMES_YOLO_MODE"]="true" at runtime to bypass all checks
- BUG-002 (HIGH): replace substring "APPROVE" in answer with exact
  answer == "APPROVE" in _smart_approve; prompt already requests exactly
  one word, substring match was exploitable via verbose LLM responses
- BUG-001 (MEDIUM): add logger.warning for every dangerous command that
  auto-approves in non-interactive non-gateway context; makes silent
  approvals visible in audit logs without breaking script behavior
- BUG-008 (LOW): expand curl/wget pipe pattern to cover | /bin/bash and
  | bash -c variants, not just | sh / | bash

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 4.6 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(approval): add missing is_truthy_value import + fix yolo test patches

_YOLO_MODE_FROZEN uses is_truthy_value() from utils — import was missing.
Tests that set HERMES_YOLO_MODE via monkeypatch.setenv() no longer work
because the value is frozen at import time; update them to patch the
module-level flag direc

title: Align approval and patch-safety decisions with the effective split filesystem policy
before: At parent c1ea3f95d13a851889d78a3d7ca7946162662c99, several core approval consumers still classified filesystem restriction through the legacy SandboxPolicy projection. Unmatched-command fallback and default execution approval derived allow/prompt behavior from legacy categories; shell, unified-exec, and intercepted-exec requests did not consistently supply the split filesystem policy to that decision boundary. Patch write safety also locally reconstructed readable and writable-root semantics instead of using the shared effective-access query. This allowed approval and patch-safety logic to diverge from the split policy carrying the actual filesystem carveouts.
after: At c2d5458d67714b9d92dfe18d8ebbb512001252d9, execution approval decisions consume FileSystemSandboxPolicy directly: restricted access requires or permits escalation prompts as appropriate, while unrestricted or externally sandboxed access follows the non-restricted path. The effective policy is threaded through shell, unified-exec, orchestration, and intercepted-exec call sites. Patch write eligibility delegates to the shared can_write_path_with_cwd query. Regression tests establish that legacy sandbox_mode configurations construct equivalent split filesystem/network policies and round-trip without semantic drift, and that a restricted split policy controls escalation even when the legacy projection says danger-full-access.
diff: The commit modifies nine core files (259 insertions, 76 deletions). It adds FileSystemSandboxPolicy to ExecApprovalRequest and intercepted-exec context, changes unmatched fallback and default approval classification to FileSystemSandboxKind, updates shell/orchestrator/unified-exec callers to pass the effective split policy, replaces manual patch-path calculations with can_write_path_with_cwd, and adds or updates regression tests for legacy-policy conversion, restricted approval behavior, and split-policy-driven unmatched-command escalation.

    ## Why This PR Exists
    
    This PR is intentionally narrower than the title may suggest.
    
    Most of the original split-permissions migration already landed in the
    earlier `#13434 -> #13453` stack. In particular:
    
    - `#13439` already did the broad runtime plumbing for split filesystem
    and network policies.
    - `#13445` already moved `apply_patch` safety onto filesystem-policy
    semantics.
    - `#13448` already switched macOS Seatbelt generation to split policies.
    - `#13449` and `#13453` already handled Linux helper and bubblewrap
    enforcement.
    - `#13440` already introduced the first protocol-side helpers for
    deriving effective filesystem access.
    
    The reason this PR still exists is that after the follow-on
    `[permissions]` work and the new shared precedence helper in `#14174`, a
    few core approval paths were still deciding behavior from the legacy
    `SandboxPolicy` projection instead of the split filesystem policy that
    actually carries the carveouts.
    
    That means this PR is mostly a cleanup and alignment pass over the
    remaining core consumers, not a fresh sandbox backend migration.
    
    ## What Is Actually New Here
    
    - make unmatched-command fallback decisions consult
    `FileSystemSandboxPolicy` instead of only legacy `DangerFullAccess` /
    `ReadOnly` / `WorkspaceWrite` categories
    - thread `file_system_sandbox_policy` into the shell, unified-exec, and
    intercepted-exec approval paths so they all use the same split-policy
    semantics
    - keep `apply_patch` safety on the same effective-access rules as the
    shared protocol helper, rather than letting it drift through
    compatibility projections
    - add loader-level regression coverage proving legacy `sandbox_mode`
    config still builds split policies and round-trips back without semantic
    drift
    
    ## What This PR Does Not Do
    
    This PR does not introduce new platform backend enforcement on its own.
    
    - Linux backend parity remains in `#14173`.
    - Windows fail-closed handling remains in `#14172`.
    - The shared precedence/model changes live in `#14174`.
    
    ## Files To Focus On
    
    - `core/src/exec_policy.rs`: unmatched-command fallback and approval
    rendering now read the split filesystem policy directly
    - `core/src/tools/sandboxing.rs`: default exec-approval requirement keys
    off `FileSystemSandboxPolicy.kind`
    - `core/src/tools/handlers/shell.rs`: shell approval requests now carry
    the split filesystem policy
    - `core/src/unified_exec/process_manager.rs`: unified-exec approval
    requests now carry the split filesystem policy
    - `core/src/tools/runtimes/shell/unix_escalation.rs`: intercepted exec
    fallback now uses the same split-policy approval semantics
    - `core/src/safety.rs`: `apply_patch` safety keeps using effective
    filesystem access rather than legacy sandbox categories
    - `core/src/config/config_tests.rs`: new regression coverage for legacy
    `sandbox_mode` no-drift behavior through the split-policy loader
    
    ## Notes
    
    - `core/src/codex.rs` and `core/src/codex_tests.rs` are just small
    fallout updates for `RequestPermissionsResponse.scope`; they are not the
    point of the PR.
    - If you reviewed the earlier `#13439` / `#13445` stack, the main review
    question here is simply: “are there any remaining approval or
    patch-safety paths that still reconstruct semantics from legacy
    `SandboxPolicy` instead of consuming the split filesystem policy
    directly?”

title: Route shell substitution through reviewable permission decisions with visible warnings
before: At parent commit 5ad5301805ef4aef2abc15596412c54e017c28eb, the permission manager and monitor tool could hard-deny commands containing $(), backticks, <(), or >(). In the permission manager, this happened only when surrounding rules caused full evaluation, so the same substitution could be approvable as a standalone command but denied inside a compound command with an unrelated matching rule. Hard denial also prevented YOLO-mode override. Some substitution shapes outside command AST nodes, and env-prefix substitutions removed by shell-wrapper stripping, could instead be misclassified as read-only and automatically allowed. Execution confirmations had no warnings contract or warning rendering.
after: At a5ec1af301c432622e165ae18dac606e10662113, substitution-bearing agent shell and monitor commands are treated as non-read-only and normally resolve to ask rather than an implicit hard deny, while explicit deny rules retain precedence. Detection covers raw and wrapper-stripped commands, AST substitutions in every statement-node type, and the regex fallback path. Shell and monitor confirmations attach a shared informational warning for substitution, and the CLI renders warning-colored, prefixed text while reserving wrap-aware terminal height so approval options remain visible.
diff: Removed substitution-specific default-deny branches from the permission manager and monitor permission resolver; narrowed the manager's default result to allow or ask; hoisted AST substitution rejection above node-type dispatch; added pre-strip/raw substitution protection to shell permission and fallback read-only checks; introduced shared substitution detection and warning helpers plus an optional warnings field on execution confirmation details; populated warnings in shell and monitor call sites; rendered warnings in the terminal confirmation component with wrapped-row height accounting; and added regression tests for standalone and compound commands, all four substitution syntaxes, wrapper/env-prefix cases, explicit-deny precedence, warning generation/rendering, AST blind spots, and constrained layouts.

fix(permissions): make command substitution ask, not deny (#4093) (#4386)

* fix(permissions): make command substitution ask, not deny (#4093)

`resolveDefaultPermission` hard-denied any shell command containing
$(), backticks, <(), or >(). Two problems:

1. The deny couldn't be overridden by YOLO mode — YOLO sees the
   result only as `'ask'` or `'default'`, never `'deny'`.
2. It fired inconsistently: only when `hasRelevantRules()` happened
   to be true. A compound command like
   `echo hello && python3 -c "print($(echo hello))"` was hard-denied
   because `echo hello` matched an unrelated allow rule and made
   `hasRelevantRules()` true, while the same `python3` sub-command
   in isolation kept its L3 `'ask'` (PM skipped) and was approvable.
   Same substitution, opposite verdict — purely a function of which
   unrelated rules were loaded.

This is the surviving half of a two-step migration. `fb7e30ad3
"fix(shell): remove command substitution deny check from
getDefaultPermission"` removed the equivalent L3 deny but missed
the L4 mirror — this commit completes that cleanup.

What changes:
- `resolveDefaultPermission` no longer special-cases substitution; the
  AST read-only check already marks substitution-bearing commands as
  non-read-only, so they fall through to `'ask'` with everything else.
- Return type narrowed from `'allow' | 'ask' | 'deny'` to `'allow' | 'ask'`.
- `ToolExecuteConfirmationDetails` gains an optional `warnings?: string[]`
  field. `ShellToolInvocation.getConfirmationDetails` populates it with a
  "Contains command substitution …" line when substitution is detected
  on either the original or stripped command. The CLI confirmation
  dialog renders these as ⚠-prefixed lines in the warning color,
  mirroring Claude Code's UX (see issue thread for reference).

Out of scope: `checkCommandPermissions` in shell-utils.ts still hard-
denies substitution. That path is exercised by user-authored `!{...}`
shell injections in slash commands (shellProcessor.ts) and is a
prompt-injection defense, not the agent-tool path #4093 describes.

Regression coverage:
- permission-manager.test.ts: new `command substitution (issue #4093)`
  describe with 5 cases — standalone $(), the exact compound from the
  issue, backticks, <(), and deny-rule precedence.
- shell.test.ts: new `command substitution warning (issue #4093)`
  describe with 4 cases — $()/backticks/<() each surface a warning,
  plain commands do not.
- ToolConfirmationMessage.test.tsx: 2 new render tests.

* fix(cli): reserve warnings height in exec confirmation layout (#4386 review)

Addresses two round-1 findings from Copilot on PR #4386:

1. ToolConfirmationMessage: the warnings block was rendered as a sibling
   *below* the MaxSizedBox-capped command body (with marginTop=1), but
   the height budget computed by availableBodyContentHeight() — and the
   compactMode cap of COMPACT_BODY_MAX_LINES — didn't account for the
   extra lines. On small terminals + compactMode this could push the
   options list off-screen. Reserve the warnings footprint
   (`warningsCount + 1` for marginTop) up-front so the overall exec
   block respects availableTerminalHeight / COMPACT_BODY_MAX_LINES.

   Added a regression test (`keeps options visible alongside the
   warning on a tight compactMode layout`) that renders a substitution
   command with `availableTerminalHeight=10` + `compactMode=true` and
   asserts both the warning text and all three compactMode option
   labels remain on-screen.

2. permission-manager.test.ts: the new `command substitution (issue
   #4093)` describe had a misleading inline comment that conflated the
   issue's original scenario (`echo hello && python3 ...` + `Bash(echo *)`)
   with the test fixture (`git status && python3 ...` + `Bash(git *)`).
   Rewrote it to describe what the test actually does (`git status`
   matches `Bash(git *)`, making hasRelevantRules() true; the python3
   sub-command then resolves via resolveDefaultPermission).

* fix(permissions): align monitor + propagate warnings to ACP/non-interactive (#4386 review)

Addresses round-2 review findings from wenshao on PR #4386. Four
related findings, all about sibling drift from the original #4093 fix:
either the same hard-deny-on-substitution pattern in a sibling tool, or
downstream consumers that don't propagate the new warnings field.

1. monitor.ts: `MonitorToolInvocation.getDefaultPermission()` had the
   identical `detectCommandSubstitution → 'deny'` pattern that the
   original PR removed from `PermissionManager.resolveDefaultPermission`
   — sibling drift the original audit missed. Same UX problems apply
   (YOLO unbypassable, opaque deny). Removed the deny branch, added
   the substitution warning in `getConfirmationDetails` (mirroring
   ShellToolInvocation), updated the 5 existing tests that asserted
   the old 'deny' to assert 'ask', and added a confirmation-warning
   test for the issue #4093 mirror case. Monitor still maintains its
   separate permission boundary (Monitor(...) rules don't share with
   Bash(...) — documented in the unchanged comment at the top of
   getConfirmationDetails); only the substitution-deny half is removed.

2. ACP `buildPermissionRequestContent` (permissionUtils.ts): had no
   `exec` branch, so the new `warnings` field never reached ACP
   clients (IDE integrations etc.). Added an `exec` branch that emits
   one `⚠ <warning>` text content per warning, alongside the existing
   `edit` (diff) and `plan` (text) branches. Two regression tests
   added: warning present → ⚠ content entry; no warnings → empty.

3. Non-interactive `permissionController.buildPermissionSuggestions`:
   the `case 'exec'` description string didn't read `warnings`, so
   daemon/API consumers that delegate the approval decision back to
   a user lost the substitution context. Appended warnings as a
   parenthesized `⚠ ...` suffix to the description string. (No test
   file exists for this controller — change is small and verifiable
   by inspection; adding test scaffolding is out of scope for this
   round.)

4. Test coverage: the `command substitution (issue #4093)` describe
   blocks in `shell.test.ts` and `permission-manager.test.ts` covered
   `$()`, backticks, and `<()` but not `>()` — even though
   `detectCommandSubstitution` and the warning text both list it.
   Added a `>()` case to each block to close the regression gap.

* fix(cli): wrap-aware warnings reservation + load-bearing regression test (#4386 self-review)

Two related self-review findings from my pre-push review on PR #4386:

1. SR-1: the round-1 layout regression test
   (`keeps options visible alongside the warning on a tight compactMode
   layout`) used a single-line command at `contentWidth=80`. `MaxSizedBox`
   clamps to `min(content_lines, maxHeight)`, so a 1-line command
   renders as 1 line regardless of whether `bodyContentHeight -=
   warningsHeight` is applied — the test would still pass if that line
   were silently removed. Replaced with a 4-line command and an
   assertion on the `... N lines hidden ...` truncation footer that
   MaxSizedBox emits *only* when its cap is actually active. Confirmed
   RED → fix → GREEN: the new test fails when the warnings
   subtraction is removed and passes when restored.

2. SR-2: the warnings-height reservation reserved `warningsCount + 1`
   lines (one per warning + one marginTop separator). On narrow
   terminals the warning text wraps across multiple visual rows, so
   the reservation under-counts. Replace the per-warning `+1` with
   `ceil((warning.length + 2) / max(contentWidth, 1))` to account for
   each warning's actual rendered row count. The `+ 2` accounts for
   the `⚠ ` prefix; the `max(...,1)` keeps the math defined for
   pathological inputs. Independently flagged by Codex during
   self-review as `[P3] Account for wrapped warning lines`.

* fix(core): log substitution audit trail on YOLO/auto bypass (#4386 review)

Round-3 review caught a real observability gap: when `needsConfirmation`
returns false (YOLO mode at line 1791, or auto-approve at line 1740),
the scheduler skips `getConfirmationDetails()` entirely and the
substitution warning generated there never reaches the user. Pre-#4093
this didn't matter because substitution hard-denied before reaching
the bypass; post-#4093 it executes silently with no audit trail.

YOLO/auto by design execute arbitrary LLM-emitted commands without
warnings — bypassing the substitution warning isn't a new
vulnerability vs. e.g. an unwarned `rm -rf /tmp/x`. But operators
troubleshooting a prompt-injection incident need an audit trail.

Adds a module-level `maybeLogSubstitutionBypass()` helper that emits a
`debugLogger.warn` only when (a) the canonical tool name is in the
shell-like audit set (RUN_SHELL_COMMAND / MONITOR) AND (b) the command
arg contains substitution. Called from both bypass branches with a
`yolo` / `auto-approve` discriminator so the audit log identifies
which path bypassed.

DEBUG-only — silent at default verbosity, no noise for typical YOLO
users; forensic signal lives in `DEBUG=*` traces. No separate test
added: `debugLogger` is module-private (created at the top of
coreToolScheduler.ts), and mocking the createDebugLogger module is
disproportionate complexity for a DEBUG-only audit signal whose
logic is a 7-line guard chain.

* refactor(core): extract substitution warning constant + helper, plus permissionController test (#4386 review)

Round-3 review cleanup, bundling 4 small related findings:

1. **Extract `COMMAND_SUBSTITUTION_WARNING` constant** (`shell-utils.ts`).
   The user-facing warning string was hardcoded identically in two
   source files (`shell.ts`, `monitor.ts`); tests assert via regex so
   the constant doesn't break them. Co-located with
   `detectCommandSubstitution` since they share the same domain.

2. **Extract `buildShellExecWarnings()` helper** (`shell-utils.ts`).
   The 6-line warnings-building pattern was duplicated between
   `ShellToolInvocation.getConfirmationDetails` and
   `MonitorToolInvocation.getConfirmationDetails` — same two-input
   substitution check (stripped + raw command), same literal push,
   same undefined-on-empty contract. Both call sites collapse to a
   one-liner. This is a mechanism lift, not a boilerplate lift —
   the helper captures non-trivial behavior. The
   `checkCommandPermissions` path in `shell-utils.ts` intentionally
   keeps its own deny-reason string (different code path, different
   threat model — prompt-injection defense for `!{…}` slash commands).

3. **Drop unnecessary non-null assertion** in
   `ToolConfirmationMessage.tsx`. Line 268 already defines
   `const warnings = executionProps.warnings ?? []`; the JSX block was
   using `executionProps.warnings!.map(...)` which (a) reaches past
   the null-safe local and (b) misleads readers about whether the
   field is actually guaranteed-defined.

4. **Add `permissionController.test.ts`** covering the
   `buildPermissionSuggestions` exec branch added in commit 7bb420562.
   Seven cases: warning-present (single + multiple), non-string
   filtering, warning-absent (missing key + empty array + malformed
   non-array), and the null-payload return for invalid input. No test
   file existed for this controller before; the new file establishes
   the pattern for the four sibling controllers, but stays scoped to
   only the method under review.

* fix(core): close AST substitution gaps and log AST parser failures (#4386 R4)

Round-4 critical findings from wenshao:

1. **AST substitution blind spots in non-`command` node types** —
   `evaluateStatementReadOnly` (shellAstParser.ts) only checked
   `containsCommandSubstitutionAST` inside the `command` node branch.
   Substitution living in OTHER node types slipped through as
   read-only, causing `resolveDefaultPermission` to return `'allow'`
   and `coreToolScheduler` to auto-approve silently. Verified blind
   spots (tests added):
     - `variable_assignment` / `variable_assignments`:
       `FOO=$(curl evil)` and `FOO=$(cat /etc/shadow) ls` were read-only
     - Backtick form: `FOO=\`cat /etc/shadow\`` was read-only

   The pre-PR #4386 regex check in `resolveDefaultPermission` was a
   safety net masking these AST gaps; removing it without patching
   the AST was a real security regression.

   Fix: hoist the `containsCommandSubstitutionAST` guard to the top
   of `evaluateStatementReadOnly` so every node type inherits the
   check in one place. Net behavior: substitution anywhere in the
   statement subtree marks the whole statement as non-read-only,
   matching the contract the function's docstring (and the comment
   in `resolveDefaultPermission`) already claimed.

   Tests follow Step 7.1 RED → fix → GREEN ordering: confirmed each
   of the 3 affected shapes was misclassified as read-only before
   the AST hoist, and all 4 cases pass after.

2. **Silent catch in `resolveDefaultPermission`** — the `try/catch`
   around `isShellCommandReadOnlyAST` swallowed parser exceptions
   without logging. With the regex safety net gone, the AST check is
   now the sole gatekeeper, so a parser regression would silently
   route every command to 'ask' with no trace. Added the same
   `debugLogger.warn` already used by the equivalent catches in
   `shell.ts` (line 1394) and `monitor.ts` (line 192).

3. **Misleading comment** in `resolveDefaultPermission` already
   asserted "the AST walker marks any node with a substitution
   expansion as non-read-only" — true post-fix, but false pre-fix.
   Updated to reference the load-bearing top-level guard in
   `shellAstParser.ts` so the claim is verifiable from one place.

Closes wenshao R4 findings: AST blind spots (`permission-manager.ts:417`
+ `shellAstParser.ts:884`), silent catch (`permission-manager.ts:415`).

* fix(core): extend substitution audit log + dual-check stripped form (#4386 R4)

Round-4 audit-log consistency fixes from wenshao:

1. **Dual-check stripped form in audit predicate** — round 3's
   `maybeLogSubstitutionBypass` only ran `detectCommandSubstitution`
   on the raw command, but `buildShellExecWarnings` (the
   confirmation-dialog warning helper extracted in round 3) checks
   BOTH the raw and the `stripShellWrapper`-stripped forms. For
   wrappers like `bash -c 'echo $(cat secret)'` the `$(` sits inside
   the outer single quotes, so raw-check returns false but the inner
   shell still expands the substitution. Result: dialog showed the
   warning, audit log silently dropped it — exactly the wrapper
   pattern an exfiltration attack would use. Refactored the helper
   to extract a pure predicate `shouldAuditSubstitutionBypass` that
   does the dual-check, exported for unit testing.

2. **JSDoc correction** — round 3's JSDoc claimed "DEBUG-level log
   here so the signal exists when `DEBUG=*` is set". Both clauses
   were wrong: the call uses `debugLogger.warn` (WARN level), and
   `debugLogger` is controlled by `QWEN_DEBUG_LOG_FILE` (active by
   default) rather than the `DEBUG=*` convention of the `debug` npm
   package. Rewrote the doc to match the real semantics.

3. **Audit log on three more auto-approve bypass paths** — round 3
   only covered the YOLO and auto-mode-`approved` bypasses, missing
   three other paths that auto-approve without invoking
   `getConfirmationDetails()`:
     - PM `'allow'` fast path (coreToolScheduler.ts:1664) — fires
       when an allow rule matches a substitution-bearing command
       (e.g. `allow Bash(python3 *)` + `python3 -c "$(...)"`).
     - permission-request hook `shouldAllow` (line ~1896) — fires
       when an external hook grants permission directly.
     - `autoApproveCompatiblePendingTools` sibling-tool ProceedAlways
       (line ~3300) — fires when one tool's user-issued ProceedAlways
       outcome rolls up to a sister tool. Uses `canonicalToolName`
       to normalise the legacy name in the audit log.

   New `SubstitutionBypassReason` discriminator union surfaces the
   bypass path in the log so operators can distinguish them.

4. **Unit test coverage** — added a `shouldAuditSubstitutionBypass`
   describe block to `coreToolScheduler.test.ts` covering all 8
   branches: non-shell tool, missing args, non-string command,
   absent substitution, direct substitution (shell + monitor), the
   load-bearing wrapper case (proves the dual-check works), backtick
   substitution, and env-prefix substitution.

Out of scope: reviewer also suggested forcing `'ask'` whenever
substitution is detected with a matching allow rule. Declined —
would partially re-introduce #4093 (substitution can't be allowed
via rules even with explicit user intent), and overrides the
allow-rule "trust this pattern" semantics. The audit-log extension
above gives operators the visibility they asked for without
overriding user-configured permission policy.

Closes wenshao R4 findings: dual-check (cids 3293074365, 3293075616),
JSDoc level/envvar (cids 3293074371, 3293075619), audit on PM-allow
(cid 3293078740 — partial), audit on hook + sibling-auto (rid 4351040390
non-diff), and test coverage for the predicate (cid 3293078758 — partial).

* test(core): cover env-prefix substitution + buildShellExecWarnings dual-check (#4386 R4)

Round-4 test-coverage findings from wenshao:

1. **env-prefix integration test in `shell.test.ts`** (cid 3293075622) —
   the `command substitution warning (issue #4093)` describe block in
   `shell.test.ts` covered `$()`, backticks, `<()`, `>()`, and the
   no-warning case, but had no test for the shape where
   `stripShellWrapper` strips the env-prefix + `bash -c` wrapper to
   yield a substitution-free inner command (`echo ok`) while the raw
   command has substitution in the env assignment
   (`FOO=$(cat secret.txt) bash -c 'echo ok'`). This is the exact
   shape that exercises the `|| detectCommandSubstitution(rawCommand)`
   branch of `buildShellExecWarnings` via integration through
   `getConfirmationDetails`. Without this test, removing the `||`
   clause wouldn't regress any case here.

2. **`buildShellExecWarnings` unit tests in `shell-utils.test.ts`**
   (cid 3293078758 second half) — round 3 extracted
   `buildShellExecWarnings` as an exported helper but added no direct
   unit test. Added a 5-case describe block covering: no substitution,

   a sanity-check that the stripped form actually lacks `$(` to make
   the dual-check load-bearing), backticks, and process substitution.

   monitor.test.ts which exercise the helper through the tool

Closes wenshao R4 findings: env-prefix integration test
(cid 3293075622), `buildShellExecWarnings` direct unit coverage
(cid 3293078758 — second half).

* fix(test): drop duplicate ToolNames import in coreToolScheduler.test (#4386 R4 CI)

Round-4 commit a24485029 added `import { ToolNames }` without checking
the file already had `import { ToolNames, ToolNamesMigration }` at line
35. Vitest's esbuild was permissive about the duplicate (silently used
the latter) so the test file passed locally and `npx tsc --noEmit` on
the package didn't complain either — but CI's `tsc --build` is strict
and errored with TS2300 "Duplicate identifier 'ToolNames'", taking down
Lint + all three test platforms + Coverage in one go (run 26382523711).

Removed the duplicate import. Verified locally via `rm -rf
packages/core/dist && npx tsc --build` (clean) + `npx vitest run`
(171/171 pass).

* fix(core): close env-prefix wrapper substitution bypass at L3 (#4386 R6)

Round-6 review caught a real Critical security regression my R0 +
R4 audits both missed.

**The bug.** `ShellToolInvocation.getDefaultPermission()` calls
`stripShellWrapper(this.params.command)` BEFORE the AST check. For
`FOO=$(curl evil) bash -c 'echo ok'`, `stripShellWrapper` discards the
env-prefix AND unwraps the `bash -c` wrapper, yielding `echo ok` — a
substitution-free residual that the AST classifies as read-only.
Result: L3 returns `'allow'` → coreToolScheduler fast-allow at
line 1664 auto-approves silently with no confirmation dialog and no
user-visible warning.

The R4 top-level AST guard (`evaluateStatementReadOnly` ↳
`containsCommandSubstitutionAST`) only catches substitution that
survives `stripShellWrapper` to enter the parsed tree. The env-prefix
+ wrapper shape gets stripped to nothing visible, so the AST guard is
asked to inspect a clean tree and returns true. The pre-#4386 regex
`detectCommandSubstitution` in `resolveDefaultPermission` was a safety
net masking exactly this gap — R0 removed it without recognising the
strip-before-check pattern.

Probe (vitest harness, real `isShellCommandReadOnlyAST`):
```
{
  raw: "FOO=`whoami` bash -c 'ls'",
  stripped: "ls",
  ast_on_stripped: true,   // ← classifies as read-only
  ast_on_raw: false        // ← R4 guard works on raw
}
```

**The fix — `hasShellSubstitution` single source of truth.**
Extracted dual-check predicate (`detectCommandSubstitution(raw) ||
detectCommandSubstitution(stripShellWrapper(raw))`) into
`shell-utils.ts hasShellSubstitution(rawCommand)`. The raw arm catches
the env-prefix-wrapper shape; the stripped arm catches the inside-
single-quoted-wrapper-body shape that R3 already documented. Single
predicate keeps detection semantics in lockstep across all surfaces.

Gates added at:
- `ShellToolInvocation.getDefaultPermission` (shell.ts:1384) — primary
  fix for the cited bug
- `shellReadOnlyChecker.ts evaluateShellSegment` (line 298) — regex
  fallback path has the same strip-before-check pattern; only hit when
  WASM parser fails, but same root cause
- `MonitorToolInvocation.getDefaultPermission` (monitor.ts:174) —
  belt-and-suspenders; `normalizeMonitorShellCommand`'s `safetyCommand`
  preserves env-prefix tokens so the AST already sees substitution
  there, but the gate parallels shell.ts in case
  `normalizeMonitorShellCommand`'s env-preservation ever regresses
- `PermissionManager.resolveDefaultPermission` (permission-manager.ts:413)
  — belt-and-suspenders; the raw command reaches the AST already, but
  the reviewer-requested gate makes the intent grep-discoverable

Refactor (Finding C, cid 3298521063): `buildShellExecWarnings` and
`shouldAuditSubstitutionBypass` both now delegate to
`hasShellSubstitution`, addressing the reviewer's concern that the
audit-log path and the UI-warning path were maintaining parallel
dual-check implementations that could silently diverge.

**Test-first per skill Step 7.1.** Two new tests in `shell.test.ts`
under `getDefaultPermission and getConfirmationDetails`:
- `asks (not allow) for env-prefix substitution inside a bash wrapper`
- `asks for backtick env-prefix substitution inside a bash wrapper`

Both confirmed RED pre-fix (`expected "ask" got "allow"`); GREEN
post-fix. Wider sweep (1262 tests across 19 files in permissions,
tools, utils, core, cli) all green; tsc --build clean (matching CI's
strict build).

Out of scope for this commit (deferred to follow-up #4509):
- R6 Finding B (dead catch blocks in resolveDefaultPermission / shell /
  monitor) — appended to #4509
- R6 Finding D (Record<string, unknown> cast in permissionController
  exec branch — could use discriminated-union narrow) — appended to #4509
- R6 Finding E (O(N×D) DFS in evaluateStatementReadOnly — could be
  hoisted to isShellCommandReadOnlyAST as O(N) root-level check) —
  appended to #4509

Closes wenshao R6 findings: env-prefix wrapper bypass (cid 3298521039 —
Critical, fixed) + dual-check DRY (cid 3298521063 — fixed as side
effect of A's refactor).

* revert: remove substitution audit-log infrastructure (#4386 cleanup)

Reverts:
- fd2cf080d "fix(core): log substitution audit trail on YOLO/auto bypass"
- a24485029 "fix(core): extend substitution audit log + dual-check stripped form"

The audit-log infrastructure was originally added in R3 as a self-Codex
suggestion (forensic visibility when YOLO bypasses the substitution
warning) and extended in R4 to PM-allow / hook / sibling-auto paths.
None of this is what issue #4093 asked for — #4093 is purely about
making substitution `'ask'` instead of `'deny'` so YOLO can override

Each subsequent review round (R4/R5/R6/R7) then surfaced sibling-drift
findings on this infrastructure — PM-allow audit, hook audit, ACP

Removing the infrastructure removes the surface entirely.

`hasShellSubstitution` (added in 5a5cfb4fc) is kept — it's still used
by `shell.ts` L3 substitution gate and `buildShellExecWarnings`, both

* cleanup: remove out-of-scope additions from R2/R3/R6 review (#4386)

Surgical reverts that complement a5d9f087e (audit-log infrastructure
revert). These changes were accepted in earlier review rounds but were
out of scope for issue #4093 — a bug-fix PR whose stated goal is to
make command substitution `'ask'` instead of `'deny'` so YOLO can

Anything beyond that fix is unrelated to the bug and not this PR's

Removed:

1. **ACP `permissionUtils.ts`: `exec` branch in

* fix(permissions): make command substitution ask, not deny (#4093)

`resolveDefaultPermission` hard-denied any shell command containing
$(), backticks, <(), or >(). Two problems:

1. The deny couldn't be overridden by YOLO mode — YOLO sees the
   result only as `'ask'` or `'default'`, never `'deny'`.
2. It fired inconsistently: only when `hasRelevantRules()` happened
   to be true. A compound command like
   `echo hello && python3 -c "print($(echo hello))"` was hard-denied
   because `echo hello` matched an unrelated allow rule and made
   `hasRelevantRules()` true, while the same `python3` sub-command
   in isolation kept its L3 `'ask'` (PM skipped) and was approvable.
   Same substitution, opposite verdict — purely a function of which
   unrelated rules were loaded.

This is the surviving half of a two-step migration. `fb7e30ad3
"fix(shell): remove command substitution deny check from
getDefaultPermission"` removed the equivalent L3 deny but missed
the L4 mirror — this commit completes that cleanup.
