evidence_units.claim: Commit 39ee5fee identifies the defect as Shift+P conflicting with typing capital P and selects Ctrl+Alt+P while avoiding Ctrl+Shift+P and Shift+Alt+P conflicts.
The parent implementation registers the plan-mode toggle as pi.registerShortcut(Key.shift("p"), ...) and invokes togglePlanMode from its handler.
The resolved implementation registers the same description and togglePlanMode handler with Key.ctrlAlt("p").
The behavioral code diff changes only the registered key identifier from Key.shift("p") to Key.ctrlAlt("p"); the shortcut handler remains the plan-mode toggle.
Extension shortcut dispatch iterates registered shortcuts, passes each identifier to matchesKey, invokes the matching handler, and consumes the input.
The typed key API supports Ctrl+Alt combinations: Key.ctrlAlt constructs a ctrl+alt key identifier, and matchesKey combines Ctrl and Alt modifier bits before matching letter input.
The key matcher recognizes Shift plus a letter from uppercase legacy input, establishing why Shift+P overlaps with ordinary capital-P entry.
The extension runner normalizes registered shortcut identifiers, rejects built-in reserved conflicts, and exposes accepted shortcuts for interactive dispatch.
The plan-mode source comment and README are updated from Shift+P to Ctrl+Alt+P, keeping user-facing shortcut guidance aligned with registration.

Repository inspection confirms that no test file changed in the resolution commit; validation evidence for this episode is therefore limited to the existing typed key/matching contract and static before/after inspection, not a new shortcut regression test or recorded runtime check.
The changelog records that the plan-mode example shortcut changed to avoid conflict with typing capital P.

evidence_units.claim: Commit c353fbbfa3d7418920044fd194c53c970624955f is the implementation-bearing resolution linked to issue/PR 2011 and has parent 6fdd7154587c731fbffaf416cb20b8336b52b662.
evidence_units.source: git show --format=fuller c353fbbfa3d7418920044fd194c53c970624955f; issue-bundle.json linked_pull_requests[0].commits and parent_commit

evidence_units.claim: The parent had no RETRY_LAST command or Ctrl+Y binding; the change adds Command.RETRY_LAST and maps it to key 'y' with ctrl true.
InputPrompt checks the normalized RETRY_LAST matcher, calls the UI retry action, and returns before later input handlers can consume the event.
The retry operation is exposed as handleRetryLastPrompt in UIActions, supplied by AppContainer from useGeminiStream.retryLastPrompt, and consumed by InputPrompt.

The stream hook adds refs for the last prepared prompt and whether it errored, stores the final prepared query before sending it, marks failures on streamed and thrown errors, and resets the failure flag on successful completion or a new submission.

retryLastPrompt is a guarded operation: it does nothing while responding or waiting for confirmation, emits an informational message when there is no stored failed prompt, and only otherwise proceeds with replay.

Before replay, retryLastPrompt commits the pending error text without its transient hint, clears pending retry/countdown state, and resubmits the stored prompt as a non-continuation with skipPreparation enabled.
submitQuery gains a skipPreparation option that sends the supplied stored query directly instead of invoking prepareQueryForGemini, allowing replay of the already-prepared prompt.

Error history items gain an optional hint; HistoryItemDisplay passes it to ErrorMessage, which renders it inline in secondary color, while failure paths keep the hinted error pending so the hint can be removed during retry.
The key-matcher table tests Ctrl+Y as a positive RETRY_LAST match and plain Y and Ctrl+R as negative matches, establishing modifier normalization and non-conflict with reverse search.

InputPrompt tests exercise the Ctrl+Y byte path and verify that plain Y remains normal input and Ctrl+R remains distinct; however, the positive Ctrl+Y case does not assert that handleRetryLastPrompt was called.

Stream-hook tests assert that retry errors are represented as pending error items with inline countdown hints, update as timers advance, and are cleared after successful automatic retry; another error-path test verifies a pending error item is created.
The visible shortcut list, localized strings, and user reference document describe Ctrl+Y as retrying the last failed request and provide messages for retry availability.

candidate_workflows.description: A partial-order implementation workflow that introduces an exact semantic key binding, establishes replay eligibility state, reconciles transient failure UI, and routes the shortcut to one guarded replay action.

workflow_graph.goal: A focused keyboard shortcut safely replays the exact last failed prepared operation once, while preserving normal typing, existing shortcuts, active execution flows, durable error history, and transient retry feedback.
when_to_use: A terminal or keyboard-driven interface needs an explicit shortcut to repeat the most recent failed asynchronous operation.
The application can identify and retain the exact prepared operation that failed.
The input layer already routes normalized key events through semantic command matchers and UI actions.
anti_goals: Do not make the unmodified character trigger replay or replace an existing shortcut.
Do not replay the most recent successful operation or guess a request when no failed target exists.
Do not interrupt an active response or a confirmation workflow.
Do not duplicate prompt preparation or leave transient retry hints in durable history.
Do not redesign automatic retry policy as part of adding the manual shortcut.
not_applicable_when: The operation cannot be safely or deterministically replayed from retained state.
Replay is non-idempotent or requires fresh user confirmation that the workflow cannot obtain.
The interface bypasses the normalized command-routing layer or the proposed key conflicts cannot be resolved.
Failures are already exclusively handled by an automatic retry mechanism and no manual replay affordance is desired.
inputs: A semantic command identifier and non-conflicting normalized key chord
The prepared operation payload that must be retained for replay
Explicit success/failure and active-execution state predicates
A UI action route from the focused input component to the operation controller
Transient error/hint state and durable history APIs
Matcher, input-routing, lifecycle, and replay validation harnesses
workflow_graph.entry_state: The application can submit operations and display failures, but has no semantic retry-last shortcut, retained failed-operation contract, or guarded manual replay action.
workflow_graph.exit_state: The exact shortcut dispatches one replay action; replay occurs only for an idle controller with a retained failed operation; the prior error is preserved without transient hint text; pending retry artifacts are cleared; and unrelated keys and active workflows remain unchanged.

steps.condition: The operation controller can expose the prepared payload and distinguish failed, successful, responding, and confirmation states.
steps.validation: Lifecycle tests demonstrate that only the latest failed prepared operation is eligible and active states suppress replay.

steps.condition: A failed operation is eligible and pending error or countdown UI may exist.
steps.validation: A replay test proves hint-free history preservation, clearing of pending retry state, preparation bypass, and exactly one submission of the stored payload.

steps.condition: The chosen chord is representable by the normalized matcher and is available in the focused input context.
steps.validation: Matcher tests distinguish the modified chord from plain and conflicting keys, and an input test asserts the routed replay callback is invoked exactly once.

validation_ladder: Static contract: confirm the semantic command, default chord, UI action type, provider wiring, and input dispatch branch agree.
Matcher unit tests: prove the intended modifier/key combination matches while the plain key and nearby existing shortcut do not.
Input routing test: send the terminal key sequence and assert exactly one replay action call; verify normal typing and existing shortcut behavior remain intact.
Lifecycle unit tests: cover no failed target, prior success, active response, waiting for confirmation, and eligible failed target.
State reconciliation test: prove durable error text excludes the transient hint, pending retry artifacts clear, and the prepared payload is submitted once without re-preparation.
User-contract check: ensure shortcut discovery, documentation, and localized availability messages describe the implemented behavior.
stop_conditions: Stop if the exact failed prepared operation cannot be retained without ambiguity.
Stop if the selected key chord conflicts with an existing command in the same input context.
Stop if replay can run concurrently with active execution or confirmation.
Stop if validation cannot distinguish retrying a failed request from resubmitting arbitrary or successful input.
Stop promotion if the positive shortcut path or guarded replay operation lacks an asserting test oracle.
unresolved_or_deferred: The committed InputPrompt Ctrl+Y positive test sends the control byte but does not assert that handleRetryLastPrompt was called.
No direct useGeminiStream test in the inspected commit was found for retryLastPrompt eligibility guards, hint-free history commit, skipPreparation arguments, or exactly-once replay.
Repository tests were not executed because the supplied worktree has widespread pre-existing deletions; validation claims are based on inspected test code, not a fresh passing run.

The final implementation still maintains a separate retry_countdown item while also placing countdown text in the error hint; the intended long-term presentation contract is not fully established by this episode.

unresolved_questions: Did CI or the PR status checks pass? The evidence bundle marks status checks and review metadata unavailable.

Should manual replay bypass every preparation side effect, or only transformations already reflected in the stored prepared request? The implementation uses a single skipPreparation switch without a dedicated behavioral test.
Was the non-asserting positive Ctrl+Y InputPrompt test intentional, or did module mocking prevent verification of the dispatched callback?

title: Align grapheme-cluster width estimates with terminal cell allocation
before: At parent 2c3041242040179b63841922ac58188f8499d2cd, terminal width calculation assigned each grapheme the width of its first visible code point, with extra accounting only for trailing halfwidth/fullwidth forms and Thai/Lao AM vowels. Indic consonants following marks and most terminal-spacing marks inside a grapheme were therefore omitted, causing measured line widths to be smaller than the cells allocated by wcwidth-style terminals.
after: At dfe47d3fbd8bf27841becaf8ec042dc0e73804a6, width calculation recognizes Unicode spacing marks plus selected legacy wcwidth exceptions, counts those marks as terminal cells, and counts visible continuation characters occurring after marks. Ordinary combining marks, specified zero-width exceptions, CJK/Japanese widths, Thai/Lao behavior, and selected Myanmar zero-width combinations remain covered by regression assertions.
diff: The change added per-code-point classifiers for non-printing characters, marks, and terminal-spacing marks; handled terminal-spacing mark-only clusters before the general zero-width rule; replaced the narrow trailing-character loop with a stateful scan that counts spacing marks and visible characters following marks; and added 43 lines of width regression tests spanning Indic scripts, ordinary combining marks, CJK/Japanese text, Thai/Lao vowels, and Myanmar marks.

commit.subject: fix(tui): align grapheme widths with terminal cells (#6987)
commit.body_excerpt:
Intl.Segmenter can group Indic conjuncts and spacing marks into one grapheme even when wcwidth-style terminals allocate multiple cells. Count visible consonants after marks and Unicode spacing marks separately while preserving zero-width exceptions.

This is a compatibility heuristic. Unicode Spacing_Mark indicates positive advance, not a full terminal cell; Kitty keeps many Indic continuations in the initial cell, while xterm-style terminals advance for them, so Pi overcounts some clusters in Kitty.

Overcounting causes horizontal drift, but undercounting can trigger terminal autowrap, so this change favors overcounting.

Clusters can contain repeated marks and mark-consonant continuations, so this implementation leaves their widths uncapped. Collapsing them would undercount terminals that advance for every visible continuation.

Mode 2027 does not report cluster widths, so Pi still needs local width calculations. This change does not implement OSC 66, which would be preferable where supported.

Fixes #6124

Co-authored-by: Mario Zechner <badlogicgames@gmail.com>

commit.subject: fix(tui): restrict fast-echo bypass to ASCII so Vietnamese/CJK/IME input renders correctly (#26011)
commit.body_excerpt:
* fix(tui): restrict fast-echo bypass to ASCII so Vietnamese/CJK/IME input renders correctly

The composer's fast-echo path (canFastAppend / canFastBackspace) writes
characters straight to stdout to skip an Ink re-render on the hot
typing path. The previous guard only checked
'stringWidth(text) === text.length', which lets a lot of non-ASCII
through:

  - Vietnamese precomposed letters (ề, ắ, ờ, ự, ...) report width 1 and
    length 1, but a Vietnamese Telex / IME stack produces them across
    multiple keystrokes; the intermediate composition state must be
    drawn by Ink so the rendered cell, the stored value, and the
    cursor column stay in lockstep when the final commit replaces the
    preview.
  - NFD combining marks (U+0300..U+036F) are zero-width but length 1,
    so even a passing equality lets them slip and silently desync the
    cell column.
  - CJK/East-Asian wide and emoji rejected only because their length
    differs, but the boundary was shape-shaped, not intent-shaped.

User-visible bug from the original report:
  Example: eê noiói nge neène
  -> the bypass committed the IME preview char before the diacritic
     replaced it, leaving doubled letters on screen.

episode.title: Keep terminal fast-echo optimization on an ASCII-safe boundary
episode.before: At parent d5416284f11ccbc735c8357f0ab35ce5f683ccc3, the text input's direct-to-stdout append shortcut admitted text whenever stringWidth(text) equaled JavaScript text.length, and its direct backspace shortcut admitted any final grapheme whose display width was one cell. Those shape checks allowed width-one non-ASCII input, including precomposed Vietnamese IME output, to bypass the normal Ink render path, risking divergence among displayed cells, stored input, and cursor position.
episode.after: At 9fb40e6a3d6338b6a6a616010de7a16672148924, direct append and backspace are permitted only when the affected text is nonempty printable ASCII and the existing end-of-line, single-line, non-wrapping, focused-TTY conditions also hold. Non-ASCII, combining, wide, emoji, control, multiline, middle-edit, and wrap-boundary cases fall through to normal rendering. Exported pure eligibility helpers make this boundary directly testable.
episode.diff: The change adds a printable-ASCII predicate and two pure fast-path eligibility helpers, replaces the prior display-width equality checks at both stdout bypass call sites with those helpers, preserves the existing direct stdout writes and deferred synchronization for eligible ASCII edits, and adds a focused 19-test regression matrix covering accepted ASCII plus rejected Vietnamese, combining-mark, CJK, emoji, control, NBSP/Latin-1, cursor-position, multiline, empty-input, and wrapping cases.

evidence_units.claim: Commit 9fb40e6a is the implementation-bearing resolution for issue/PR 26011, with parent d5416284, and changes only the text-input implementation and a new focused test file.

The parent implementation admitted append text when stringWidth(text) equaled text.length and admitted backspace when the removed grapheme's stringWidth was one, in addition to the common fast-echo base and line-shape conditions.
Before the change, successful append and backspace eligibility caused direct stdout writes and commits that skipped immediate local and parent synchronization.
The new append eligibility helper requires the cursor at the end, a nonempty single-line value, printable ASCII inserted text, and a resulting line width strictly below the terminal column count.
The new backspace eligibility helper requires deletion at the end of a nonempty single-line value and admits the removed grapheme only when it consists entirely of printable ASCII.
The component combines the existing focused, unmasked, unselected TTY precondition with the new pure helpers before selecting the direct append or backspace paths.
Eligible ASCII edits retain the optimized direct stdout behavior, while failed eligibility falls through to the ordinary edit and render flow.
Append tests preserve the intended ASCII fast path and reject unsafe structural states: cursor not at end, empty placeholder state, multiline input, and an append reaching the wrap column.
Append regression tests reject precomposed Vietnamese letters, Vietnamese tone-mark letters, NFD combining marks, CJK, emoji, ANSI/control text, NBSP, and Latin-1 letters.
Backspace tests preserve deletion of a final ASCII character and reject middle-of-line or empty deletion, multiline values, Vietnamese, CJK, NFD-composed graphemes, and emoji.
The patch extracts pure eligibility helpers, replaces the two width-based guards, and adds the dedicated fast-echo regression suite without redesigning the normal renderer.

The commit message reports that the regression matrix was red under the previous guard for 11 of 20 checked cases and green under the new guard; this is author-reported validation rather than a test execution performed during extraction.

The implementation explains that display-width equality is insufficient because a precomposed Vietnamese character can have both length one and width one while still participating in multi-keystroke IME composition.

episode.title: Replace unstable emoji-width markers in terminal-visible text
episode.before: At parent 52f875a875c20e927092a8b3aeb162614797543a, terminal-visible statuses, notices, summaries, and labels used emoji or emoji-presentation sequences such as 🟢, 🟡, 🔴, 🔄, ⏳, 🔎, 🚫, 💡, ✅, ❌, 🔒, and ⚠️. These strings could occupy two terminal columns or vary by renderer. Several state indicators also depended on color, and translated message keys and documentation embedded the old markers.
episode.after: At a756676b2180bd5ba8c0062f98f140c5f0a9e732, affected strings use narrower text-presentation symbols such as ✓, ✗, ◐, ●, ◌, ◎, ★, ▸, ▷, and ⚠, or omit redundant decorative prefixes. Connected, connecting, and disconnected IDE states have distinct text shapes independent of color. Locale keys and selected documentation are reconciled with the changed strings, while tests and snapshots assert representative rendered output and explicitly drive MCP connection states.
episode.diff: The implementation-bearing commit modifies 39 files with 251 insertions and 241 deletions. It replaces or removes emoji markers across CLI rendering, emitted session messages, and formatted agent statistics; strips U+FE0F from warning/info sequences; updates nine locale files and two user documents; revises unit assertions and Ink snapshots; and repairs MCP status tests so connecting and disconnected branches are selected through the component's serverStatus input instead of an ineffective module spy. The diff also changes some non-TUI strings, including retry-loop directives and PR attribution, so the change is broader than a purely terminal-rendering patch.

evidence_units.claim: Commit a756676b2180bd5ba8c0062f98f140c5f0a9e732 is linked to issue/PR 5999, has parent 52f875a875c20e927092a8b3aeb162614797543a, and records a 39-file implementation-and-test change intended to replace width-2 emoji with text symbols.
The parent rendered MCP states and startup/tip labels with 🟢, 🔄, 🔴, ⏳, and 💡; the pinned implementation uses ●, ◐, ◌, and ★ while retaining status-dependent color properties.
IDE connection output changes from colored-circle emoji to shape-distinct text markers: ✓ for connected, ◐ for connecting, and ✗ for disconnected, in both status formatting paths.

Terminal-facing markers are normalized across multiple semantic surfaces: redundant footer lock decoration is removed, workflow activity uses ▷, vision notices use ◎, blocked/error messages use ✗, tips use ★, pending work uses ◌, and statistics use text symbols such as ▸, ●, and ✓.
Warning and information markers remove the emoji variation selector, changing sequences such as ⚠️ and ℹ️ to text-presentation ⚠ and ℹ in user-visible messages.

The changed markers are consumed directly by Ink Text nodes, command message results, history items, session message emission, and statistics formatter return strings, making them observable at terminal-rendering or terminal-message call sites.

evidence_units.claim: User documentation removes the footer lock emoji and replaces documented IDE disconnection circle emoji, demonstrating that examples were considered part of the user-visible text contract.
IDE command tests assert exact ✓ Connected, ◐ Connecting, and ✗ Disconnected output, including disconnection details and the asynchronously emitted connected message.

MCP tests now inject DISCONNECTED and CONNECTING through the serverStatus prop, and snapshots verify ◌ startup, ● stable states, ◐ connecting output, and ★ tips. The connecting snapshot changes behaviorally from an incorrectly rendered Ready state to Starting output.
Additional tests assert the new ◎ vision marker, ⚠ text-presentation warnings, ◐ hook messages, ▸/●/✓/★ statistics text, and the complete ▷ workflow-active footer label.

The LSP table test expands its negative character class to reject both prior emoji and the newly adopted text markers, preserving that surface's plain-text status vocabulary rather than applying the glyph migration indiscriminately.
The retry-loop warning strings are explicitly documented as model-facing prompt directives rather than TUI glyphs, marking a semantic boundary even though their variation selectors are also removed.

The repository contains exact-output unit and snapshot oracles for representative connection states, notices, warnings, footer output, and statistics, but the available evidence bundle contains no CI status or recorded local test execution for the pinned commit.

candidate_workflows.name: stabilize_unicode_markers_in_terminal_output
candidate_workflows.title: Stabilize Unicode markers across terminal output contracts
candidate_workflows.description: A partial-order workflow for replacing width-unstable emoji in terminal-visible output without losing state meaning, breaking translations, or creating tests that fail to exercise the intended rendering branches.

workflow_graph.goal: Make affected terminal-visible markers occupy the intended text-style columns while preserving semantic state recognition and synchronizing dependent text contracts.
when_to_use: Terminal alignment, wrapping, or spacing is unreliable because user-visible prefixes contain emoji or emoji-presentation sequences.
A status interface uses colored emoji whose width or meaning changes across terminals, CJK environments, NO_COLOR output, or copied text.
Changing a rendered marker also changes localization keys, snapshots, exact-string tests, or documented examples.
anti_goals: Do not replace every Unicode character merely because it is non-ASCII.
Do not make state meaning depend only on color or use one identical shape for semantically opposed states.
Do not alter substantive labels, state transitions, or business behavior while repairing marker width.
Do not propagate the terminal glyph vocabulary into tables, model prompts, web-only text, or other surfaces without verifying their separate presentation contract.
Do not treat updated snapshots alone as proof when the fixture does not actually select the intended state branch.
not_applicable_when: The defect is caused by an incorrect width-calculation algorithm for arbitrary user content rather than fixed application-owned markers.
The output target is not a terminal and its renderer intentionally supports emoji presentation.
No implementation, call site, or test oracle can establish which strings are terminal-visible.
The marker is user-provided content that must be preserved verbatim.
inputs: Pinned implementation ref and parent ref
Inventory of application-owned marker-bearing strings and their rendering call sites
Terminal column-width and text-presentation requirements

workflow_graph.exit_state: In-scope terminal strings use approved text-presentation symbols or no redundant marker; distinct states remain recognizable without color; affected translations, tests, snapshots, and documentation are reconciled; excluded surfaces retain their own output policy.

steps.condition: Apply only to application-owned strings confirmed to reach terminal rendering or terminal-visible message output.
steps.validation: Inspect final call sites and exact-output tests to confirm each old marker is replaced or removed without changing its substantive label.

steps.condition: Required whenever multiple semantic states previously relied on different colors or colored emoji.
steps.validation: Each state branch yields a distinct text shape and label; IDE tests assert ✓, ◐, and ✗ for connected, connecting, and disconnected states.

steps.condition: Classify adjacent output surfaces before applying replacements broadly.
steps.validation: Glyph-free surfaces have negative assertions, and non-terminal strings have explicit ownership or are deferred from terminal-width reasoning.

steps.condition: Run when markers are embedded in translation keys, translated values, user documentation, or external examples.
steps.validation: Affected locale keys and documented examples no longer rely on the superseded marker, subject to recorded documentation discrepancies.

steps.condition: Use the actual dependency-injection or prop boundary consumed by the renderer for every representative state.

candidate_workflows.name: stabilize_unicode_markers_in_terminal_output
candidate_workflows.title: Stabilize Unicode markers across terminal output contracts
candidate_workflows.description: A partial-order workflow for replacing width-unstable emoji in terminal-visible output without losing state meaning, breaking translations, or creating tests that fail to exercise the intended rendering branches.

workflow_graph.goal: Make affected terminal-visible markers occupy the intended text-style columns while preserving semantic state recognition and synchronizing dependent text contracts.
when_to_use: Terminal alignment, wrapping, or spacing is unreliable because user-visible prefixes contain emoji or emoji-presentation sequences.
A status interface uses colored emoji whose width or meaning changes across terminals, CJK environments, NO_COLOR output, or copied text.
Changing a rendered marker also changes localization keys, snapshots, exact-string tests, or documented examples.
anti_goals: Do not replace every Unicode character merely because it is non-ASCII.
Do not make state meaning depend only on color or use one identical shape for semantically opposed states.
Do not alter substantive labels, state transitions, or business behavior while repairing marker width.
Do not propagate the terminal glyph vocabulary into tables, model prompts, web-only text, or other surfaces without verifying their separate presentation contract.
Do not treat updated snapshots alone as proof when the fixture does not actually select the intended state branch.
not_applicable_when: The defect is caused by an incorrect width-calculation algorithm for arbitrary user content rather than fixed application-owned markers.
The output target is not a terminal and its renderer intentionally supports emoji presentation.
No implementation, call site, or test oracle can establish which strings are terminal-visible.
The marker is user-provided content that must be preserved verbatim.
inputs: Pinned implementation ref and parent ref
Inventory of application-owned marker-bearing strings and their rendering call sites
Terminal column-width and text-presentation requirements
State-to-label and state-to-style mapping
Locale catalogs, exact-string tests, snapshots, and documentation containing affected literals
List of output surfaces that must remain glyph-free or are not terminal-rendered
workflow_graph.entry_state: Application-owned terminal strings contain width-variable emoji or presentation selectors, and dependent state mappings or textual contracts still encode the old markers.
workflow_graph.exit_state: In-scope terminal strings use approved text-presentation symbols or no redundant marker; distinct states remain recognizable without color; affected translations, tests, snapshots, and documentation are reconciled; excluded surfaces retain their own output policy.

steps.condition: Apply only to application-owned strings confirmed to reach terminal rendering or terminal-visible message output.
steps.validation: Inspect final call sites and exact-output tests to confirm each old marker is replaced or removed without changing its substantive label.

steps.condition: Required whenever multiple semantic states previously relied on different colors or colored emoji.
steps.validation: Each state branch yields a distinct text shape and label; IDE tests assert ✓, ◐, and ✗ for connected, connecting, and disconnected states.

steps.condition: Classify adjacent output surfaces before applying replacements broadly.
steps.validation: Glyph-free surfaces have negative assertions, and non-terminal strings have explicit ownership or are deferred from terminal-width reasoning.

steps.condition: Run when markers are embedded in translation keys, translated values, user documentation, or external examples.
steps.validation: Affected locale keys and documented examples no longer rely on the superseded marker, subject to recorded documentation discrepancies.

steps.condition: Use the actual dependency-injection or prop boundary consumed by the renderer for every representative state.
steps.validation: Rendered frames or exact strings prove that stable, transitional, and failure branches emit their intended markers and labels.

Contract reconciliation: check locale keys, translated values, exact-string assertions, snapshots, and documented examples.

title: Wrap terminal markdown-table content using Unicode display widths
before: At parent a2174751de2e25c0f8b9ea4540c15cc1fcfba9c6, the table renderer measured processed plain-text lengths, proportionally scaled columns to the terminal width, and truncated over-width cells by JavaScript string index before appending an ellipsis. Each logical header or data row produced exactly one terminal line. Long headers and cells therefore lost content, and string-index truncation was not aligned with terminal display cells for emoji and East Asian scripts.
after: At 49533cd106a646d0a80da16efaf45e00d9efe108, the renderer converts content to styled characters, measures terminal display width and widest words, allocates content width within the terminal budget, wraps headers and cells into display-width-bounded lines, tightens columns to their widest resulting line, and renders every logical row as aligned visual rows padded by measured display width. Bold header delimiters are removed before wrapping because header styling is supplied by the renderer. Tests and snapshots cover long, mixed-length, punctuation-heavy, bold-header, emoji, Chinese, Japanese, Korean, and complex multi-line content.
diff: The implementation replaced plain-length proportional scaling and ellipsis truncation with a memoized constraint/allocation/wrapping pipeline based on Ink styled-character width primitives; added multi-line row rendering and header-marker normalization; upgraded the Ink dependency from 6.4.8 to 6.4.10; and added 10 test scenarios plus updated snapshots demonstrating preserved wrapped content and Unicode-aligned borders.

evidence_units.claim: Commit 49533cd106a646d0a80da16efaf45e00d9efe108 is the implementation-bearing resolution for PR/issue 18240 and has parent a2174751de2e25c0f8b9ea4540c15cc1fcfba9c6.
evidence_units.source: issue-bundle.json linked_pull_requests[0].commits[0], parent_commit, and git show --format=fuller 49533cd106a646d0a80da16efaf45e00d9efe108

evidence_units.claim: The change modifies the table renderer, its tests and snapshots, and upgrades Ink from 6.4.8 to 6.4.10; the commit reports 619 insertions and 91 deletions across six files.
evidence_units.source: git show --stat --no-renames 49533cd106a646d0a80da16efaf45e00d9efe108; package.json, packages/cli/package.json, and package-lock.json diff

evidence_units.claim: The parent renderer derived widths with getPlainTextLength, proportionally scaled them, truncated over-width strings using substring and binary search, appended an ellipsis, and rendered one line per logical row.

The new calculateWidths operation converts text to styled characters and uses styledCharsWidth, wordBreakStyledChars, and widestLineFromStyledChars to obtain display-cell content width and widest-word width.

For each column, the renderer derives minimum and maximum width constraints from the header and all cells, subtracts borders, padding, and a table margin from terminalWidth, preserves short columns when feasible, and distributes scarce or surplus width across the remaining columns.

Headers and cells are converted to styled characters, wrapped to their allocated display width, converted back to strings, and cached with measured line widths; final columns are tightened to the widest wrapped line plus padding.
Each logical row is rendered as as many visual rows as its tallest wrapped cell, with missing lines represented by empty measured cells so borders and columns remain aligned.

Bold delimiters are stripped from headers before measurement and wrapping because the renderer applies bold styling itself, preventing delimiters from being split across wrapped lines or displayed literally.
The component contract retains headers, rows, and terminalWidth as runtime inputs, so the behavioral change remains localized behind the existing table-rendering interface.

candidate_atomics.title: Allocate column widths from terminal display-cell constraints
candidate_atomics.description: Measure headers and cells in terminal display cells, establish per-column minimum and desired widths, and allocate the available terminal budget while retaining short columns when feasible.

semantic_action.intent: Give every table column a width budget based on what the terminal occupies rather than JavaScript string length, without exceeding the width available after structural overhead.

semantic_action.post_state: Each column has an allocated content width derived from display-cell measurements, widest-word constraints, terminal width, borders, padding, margin, and short-column preservation rules.

candidate_atomics.title: Wrap cells into aligned multi-line terminal rows
candidate_atomics.description: Wrap styled content to its allocated display width, cache each visual line's measured width, tighten columns to actual wrapped content, and expand logical rows into aligned visual rows instead of truncating content.

semantic_action.intent: Preserve over-width table content while keeping borders, padding, and neighboring cells aligned across every wrapped line.
semantic_action.pre_state: An over-width cell is truncated with substring and an ellipsis, and every logical row is restricted to one terminal line.
semantic_action.post_state: Every cell is represented by display-width-bounded visual lines; a logical row has the height of its tallest cell, shorter cells receive empty continuation lines, and padding uses cached display width.
semantic_action.validation: Component assertions must retain text from long cells, and snapshots must show complete content split across aligned visual rows for mixed lengths, punctuation, explicit newlines, emoji, and East Asian scripts.

candidate_workflows.name: replace-terminal-table-truncation-with-unicode-aware-wrapping
candidate_workflows.title: Replace lossy table truncation with Unicode-aware wrapping
candidate_workflows.description: A partial-order resolution workflow for terminal tables that lose long content or mismeasure emoji and East Asian text: establish a display-cell width contract, allocate columns within structural overhead, normalize renderer-owned header markup, wrap content, render aligned continuation rows, and verify representative snapshots.

workflow_graph.goal: Preserve complete markdown-table content in a bounded terminal while maintaining display-cell-correct columns and borders for ASCII, emoji, and East Asian scripts.
when_to_use: A terminal table truncates long headers or cells even though vertical wrapping is acceptable.
Column widths or padding are computed from code-unit or plain string length and become unreliable for emoji or wide scripts.
The renderer receives an explicit terminal-width budget and owns table borders, padding, and row layout.
anti_goals: Do not change the semantic contents of table cells merely to make them fit.
Do not optimize for a fixed character count when terminal display width is the relevant invariant.
Do not remove inline rendering or renderer-owned header styling.
Do not introduce horizontal scrolling or widen the terminal as a substitute for bounded wrapping.
not_applicable_when: The output surface does not have terminal display-cell width semantics.
The product explicitly requires ellipsis truncation or a single-line row contract.
No terminal-width budget or equivalent layout constraint is available.
The text system cannot preserve styling through measurement and wrapping and no compatible styled-character adapter exists.
inputs: headers and body rows
terminal-width budget
table border, separator, padding, and margin overhead
display-cell-aware styled-character measurement and wrapping primitives
header styling ownership rules
representative ASCII and Unicode rendering cases
workflow_graph.entry_state: The table fits columns by scaling measured text widths but truncates cells to one line, risking content loss and incorrect Unicode display-cell accounting.
workflow_graph.exit_state: All cells are measured and wrapped using terminal display width, logical rows expand into aligned continuation lines, renderer-owned header markup is not exposed, and committed assertions and snapshots cover long and Unicode content.

steps.validation: Calculated widths account for borders, padding, margin, widest words, full content widths, and display-cell widths rather than code-unit counts.

steps.condition: Header input may include markup for styling that the table renderer already applies structurally.
steps.validation: Literal header markers are absent from both ordinary and wrapped output while visible text and structural styling remain.

steps.condition: One or more headers or cells exceed their allocated display width, or Unicode content requires display-width-aware padding.
steps.validation: Long content remains present, each line fits its allocation, shorter sibling cells receive blank continuation lines, and snapshots show aligned borders for ASCII and Unicode cases.

validation_ladder: Unit-level assertions confirm representative fragments from long content remain instead of being ellipsized.
Header tests confirm redundant bold markers are absent before and after wrapping.
Snapshot tests verify wrapping and border alignment for single-long, all-long, mixed-length, punctuation-heavy, and complex multi-paragraph tables.
Unicode snapshots verify emoji and Chinese, Japanese, and Korean text retain content and display alignment.
Run the focused TableRenderer test suite in a materialized checkout with the pinned dependency versions; this execution remains deferred in the supplied environment.
stop_conditions: Stop if the caller requires single-line truncation rather than content preservation.
Stop if terminal display-cell measurement primitives are unavailable and cannot be introduced within scope.
Defer promotion if long-content preservation or Unicode border alignment lacks a deterministic rendering oracle.
Stop if the structural overhead alone consumes the terminal-width budget; the inspected change does not establish behavior for that pathological case.

title: Restore extension module loading inside the compiled runtime
before: At parent 53d9e61bac3408b4ff6b4ccf9dd49e1c4c9640b1, the extension loader exposed the host package to compiled-runtime extensions through a lazy require of the public index. The public index simultaneously re-exported loader functions, creating a loader-to-index-to-loader cycle. The compiled-runtime virtual module table omitted the agent-core package, the development alias table omitted the same package, and the root compilation dependency graph resolved @mariozechner/jiti 2.6.2. The changelog states that extensions with local file imports did not work correctly in the compiled Bun binary.
after: At 843f2352518cb75343f9e6e47bb86f708e1f4769, loader functions are no longer re-exported from the public index, allowing the loader to statically import the initialized public API without a circular dependency. The virtual module table now directly supplies bundled namespaces for the coding-agent API and agent-core API, while the development alias table resolves agent-core from the filesystem. The root package and lockfile select @mariozechner/jiti 2.6.5, described by the commit and changelog as bundling the transformation support required by the compiled runtime. Extension discovery and SDK/CLI call sites continue importing loader operations through the internal extensions module.
diff: The implementation removes createExtensionRuntime, discoverAndLoadExtensions, and loadExtensions from the package-root value exports; replaces the lazy public-API getter and runtime require with a static index import and direct virtual-module entry; adds agent-core to both compiled-runtime virtual modules and development aliases; and upgrades the root jiti dependency and lockfile resolution from 2.6.2 to 2.6.5. Documentation terminology was also updated, but no regression test or compiled-binary validation artifact was added in the pinned commit.

title: Make callback delivery lazy-safe and force reload lifecycle-symmetric
before: At parent eac1e25127a75c61116a0bbb8ce7681a2f8b61b4, module-level hook and middleware invocation and presence checks directly queried the process plugin manager without ensuring discovery. Processes that did not import the component whose side effect triggered discovery could therefore report no callback or silently skip delivery. Separately, full unload cleared manager-local hooks without restoring configuration-owned shell hooks, and it removed legacy platform registrations but did not deregister tool names tracked outside the ownership ledger, allowing missing configuration hooks and stale global tools after force reload.
after: At 8be9c76f8c01f652e1c7acd576c37e4bdaed30be, callback delivery entry points obtain a delivery manager that joins in-flight background discovery and performs discovery when necessary while preserving compatibility with manager test doubles. Full unload also deregisters tracked tool names not represented by tool ownership records. After a successful forced discovery sweep, configuration-owned shell hooks are rebuilt from current configuration; restoration failures are logged and do not invalidate the completed reload.
diff: The change adds a lazy-discovery delivery helper and routes module-level invoke_hook, invoke_middleware, has_hook, and has_middleware through it; adds a legacy-tool cleanup sweep during unload-all while excluding ownership-ledger tools; adds configuration-hook re-registration that resets registration idempotence and reloads configuration; invokes that reconciliation only after successful force rediscovery; and adds focused tests for lazy delivery, gate behavior, mock-manager compatibility, shell-hook restoration, fail-open restoration, and stale-tool cleanup. The commit modifies agent/shell_hooks.py, hermes_cli/plugins.py, and tests/hermes_cli/test_plugins.py with 282 insertions and 5 deletions.

commit.subject: fix(plugins): hook delivery parity + symmetric force-reload (#64178)
commit.body_excerpt:
Salvaged from PR #64188 (@Bartok9), re-reviewed against the #64229
ownership ledger (landed in #84923).

Delivery parity (survived):
- Module-level invoke_hook/invoke_middleware/has_hook/has_middleware
  lazily run plugin discovery via _delivery_manager(), so surfaces that
  never import model_tools (dashboards, TUI slash workers, query mode,
  cron, gateway platform events) deliver plugin callbacks instead of
  silently dropping them (#50776, #67597, #67890, #50937).
- _delivery_manager() joins any in-flight background discovery first and
  tolerates test doubles that monkeypatch get_plugin_manager().

Symmetric force-reload (survived):
- agent/shell_hooks.py gains re_register_config_hooks(); the force branch
  of discover_and_load() calls it after a successful sweep, restoring
  config.yaml shell hooks that the ledger-driven unload wiped but cannot
  restore (they are config-owned, not plugin-owned) (#60036).
- unload(plugin=None) now sweeps pre-ledger _plugin_tool_names entries
  out of the process-global tools.registry, mirroring the platform-name
  sweep that already existed, so zombie tools cannot survive a force
  reload in long-lived pre-ledger processes (#60050).

Supersed

commit.body_excerpt:
Salvaged from PR #64188 (@Bartok9), re-reviewed against the #64229
ownership ledger (landed in #84923).

  lazily run plugin discovery via _delivery_manager(), so surfaces that
  never import model_tools (dashboards, TUI slash workers, query mode,
  cron, gateway platform events) deliver plugin callbacks instead of
  silently dropping them (#50776, #67597, #67890, #50937).

  tolerates test doubles that monkeypatch get_plugin_manager().

  config.yaml shell hooks that the ledger-driven unload wiped but cannot
  restore (they are config-owned, not plugin-owned) (#60036).
- unload(plugin=None) now sweeps pre-ledger _plugin_tool_names entries
  out of the process-global tools.registry, mirroring the platform-name
  sweep that already existed, so zombie tools cannot survive a force
  reload in long-lived pre-ledger processes (#60050).

episode.title: Make callback delivery lazy-safe and force reload lifecycle-symmetric
episode.before: At parent eac1e25127a75c61116a0bbb8ce7681a2f8b61b4, module-level hook and middleware invocation and presence checks directly queried the process plugin manager without ensuring discovery. Processes that did not import the component whose side effect triggered discovery could therefore report no callback or silently skip delivery. Separately, full unload cleared manager-local hooks without restoring configuration-owned shell hooks, and it removed legacy platform registrations but did not deregister tool names tracked outside the ownership ledger, allowing missing configuration hooks and stale global tools after force reload.
episode.after: At 8be9c76f8c01f652e1c7acd576c37e4bdaed30be, callback delivery entry points obtain a delivery manager that joins in-flight background discovery and performs discovery when necessary while preserving compatibility with manager test doubles. Full unload also deregisters tracked tool names not represented by tool ownership records. After a successful forced discovery sweep, configuration-owned shell hooks are rebuilt from current configuration; restoration failures are logged and do not invalidate the completed reload.
episode.diff: The change adds a lazy-discovery delivery helper and routes module-level invoke_hook, invoke_middleware, has_hook, and has_middleware through it; adds a legacy-tool cleanup sweep during unload-all while excluding ownership-ledger tools; adds configuration-hook re-registration that resets registration idempotence and reloads configuration; invokes that reconciliation only after successful force rediscovery; and adds focused tests for lazy delivery, gate behavior, mock-manager compatibility, shell-hook restoration, fail-open restoration, and stale-tool cleanup. The commit modifies agent/shell_hooks.py, hermes_cli/plugins.py, and tests/hermes_cli/test_plugins.py with 282 insertions and 5 deletions.

title: Resolve extension uninstall requests by installed name or recorded source
before: At parent commit 0534ca74d4e67b00ed51e9f8bf568efc3ecaf834, uninstallExtension treated its argument strictly as an extension name. It required an exact case-sensitive match against installed.config.name, rejected source URLs or paths even when recorded in installation metadata, and then used the supplied argument directly for enablement removal, storage deletion, and uninstall telemetry. The CLI likewise described the positional argument only as an extension name.
after: At commit 2d406ffc755f79dc903c6993aae03150e1678dc0, the uninstall boundary accepts an identifier that may be either the configured extension name or installMetadata.source. It searches loaded user extensions using case-insensitive equality, safely skips absent metadata, resolves a match to the canonical configured name, and uses that canonical name for enablement removal, directory deletion, and telemetry. The CLI advertises name or source path input. Unknown identifiers, including source identifiers for installations without metadata, fail without deleting an extension.
diff: The change renamed the core input concept from extensionName to extensionIdentifier; replaced the name-only existence check with lookup by normalized configured name or normalized recorded source; retained the resolved config.name as the canonical lifecycle key; generalized the not-found error; updated CLI argument documentation; and added tests proving source-URL deletion and canonical-name telemetry while preserving name-based deletion, unrelated installations, and safe failure when metadata is absent.

episode.title: Resolve extension uninstall requests by installed name or recorded source
episode.before: At parent commit 0534ca74d4e67b00ed51e9f8bf568efc3ecaf834, uninstallExtension treated its argument strictly as an extension name. It required an exact case-sensitive match against installed.config.name, rejected source URLs or paths even when recorded in installation metadata, and then used the supplied argument directly for enablement removal, storage deletion, and uninstall telemetry. The CLI likewise described the positional argument only as an extension name.
episode.after: At commit 2d406ffc755f79dc903c6993aae03150e1678dc0, the uninstall boundary accepts an identifier that may be either the configured extension name or installMetadata.source. It searches loaded user extensions using case-insensitive equality, safely skips absent metadata, resolves a match to the canonical configured name, and uses that canonical name for enablement removal, directory deletion, and telemetry. The CLI advertises name or source path input. Unknown identifiers, including source identifiers for installations without metadata, fail without deleting an extension.
episode.diff: The change renamed the core input concept from extensionName to extensionIdentifier; replaced the name-only existence check with lookup by normalized configured name or normalized recorded source; retained the resolved config.name as the canonical lifecycle key; generalized the not-found error; updated CLI argument documentation; and added tests proving source-URL deletion and canonical-name telemetry while preserving name-based deletion, unrelated installations, and safe failure when metadata is absent.

evidence_units.claim: Commit 2d406ffc755f79dc903c6993aae03150e1678dc0 is the implementation-bearing resolution for PR/issue 8692 and has parent 0534ca74d4e67b00ed51e9f8bf568efc3ecaf834.
evidence_units.source: git show --format=fuller 2d406ffc755f79dc903c6993aae03150e1678dc0; issue-bundle.json linked_pull_requests[0].commits[0] and parent_commit

evidence_units.claim: The parent implementation accepted extensionName, checked only exact equality with installed.config.name, and used that input directly for enablement removal, storage selection, and telemetry.
evidence_units.source: git show 0534ca74d4e67b00ed51e9f8bf568efc3ecaf834:packages/cli/src/config/extension.ts, uninstallExtension implementation around lines 575-604

evidence_units.claim: The pinned diff replaces the exact name-only guard with a lookup whose predicates compare a lowercased identifier to both lowercased configured name and optional lowercased metadata source, returning the matching configured name.

The resulting implementation resolves the external identifier to config.name, rejects when no canonical name is found, and performs enablement removal, directory deletion, and successful-uninstall telemetry with that canonical name.
Installed extension loading reads install metadata and includes it on the loaded Extension object, providing the persisted source field used by identifier resolution.
Installation persists the installMetadata object, including its source, in the installed extension destination for supported copied installation types.

The uninstall command passes its positional argument unchanged to uninstallExtension, so identifier interpretation is owned by the lifecycle implementation rather than duplicated in the command handler.
The command-line positional argument description was broadened from extension name to extension name or source path.
The update lifecycle still invokes uninstallExtension with the configured extension name, demonstrating that name-based internal callers remain supported.

The source-URL test creates an installed extension with git source metadata, uninstalls using that URL, verifies the installed directory is gone, and verifies telemetry uses the canonical configured name.
The missing-metadata test supplies a URL for an installed extension without install metadata and expects 'Extension not found.', proving absent provenance is not guessed from the configured name.
Existing tests verify uninstall by configured name, preservation of unrelated extensions, not-found behavior, and successful telemetry by configured name.
The extension test fixture writes install metadata only when explicitly provided, allowing the suite to distinguish provenance-backed source resolution from installations lacking provenance.

The CLI package declares Vitest as its test runner and exposes a 'vitest run' package test command; no successful local execution result was available from the checkout because its working tree contents were already removed.

candidate_workflows.title: Support safe removal by configured identity or recorded installation source
candidate_workflows.description: Broaden a lifecycle removal boundary to accept a provenance identifier, resolve it against installed state, and preserve one canonical identity for cleanup and reporting.

workflow_graph.goal: Allow an installed extension to be safely uninstalled using either its configured name or the source recorded at installation, while keeping deletion and telemetry anchored to the canonical configured name.
when_to_use: A lifecycle command accepts only an internal or configured name, but users retain and naturally reuse the source URL or path supplied during installation.
Installed records persist provenance that can unambiguously identify the lifecycle target.
Existing cleanup subsystems require a canonical installed name rather than the external identifier.
anti_goals: Do not infer a source match from URL fragments, directory names, or configured-name similarity when persisted provenance is absent.
Do not pass a source URL or path directly into storage deletion, enablement-state removal, or telemetry as though it were the canonical installed name.
Do not broaden the change into installation, update, reload, or storage-layout redesign.
Do not remove unrelated installed extensions while resolving the requested identifier.
not_applicable_when: Installation provenance is not persisted or loaded into the installed-object model.
Multiple installed records can legitimately share the same source and no disambiguation policy exists.
The removal backend already uses an immutable identifier that callers possess, making alternate identity reconciliation unnecessary.
inputs: Removal identifier supplied by the caller
Loaded installed-extension records
Configured canonical name for each installed record
Optional persisted installation source for each installed record
Existing enablement, storage-removal, and telemetry mechanisms
workflow_graph.entry_state: The requested identifier may be a configured name or installation source, installed records are loadable, and the removal mechanisms operate on configured names; source-only requests are not yet recognized.
workflow_graph.exit_state: A request matching a configured name or recorded source removes exactly the matched extension and reports its canonical configured name; a request without an evidenced match fails before lifecycle state or storage is removed.

steps.condition: The public removal command is intended to accept the persisted installation source in addition to the configured name.
steps.validation: The argument help names both accepted identifier forms, and the command forwards the unmodified identifier to the lifecycle owner.

steps.condition: Installed records expose canonical names and optional persisted sources.
steps.validation: Source-based and name-based tests delete the intended directory; telemetry receives the canonical name; unrelated installations remain; absent metadata and unmatched identifiers produce not-found failure.

validation_ladder: Static contract check: confirm the public argument description includes configured name and source, and resolution remains centralized in the lifecycle implementation.
Resolver check: confirm matching covers normalized configured name and optional normalized persisted source and returns the configured name.
Negative unit check: confirm an unmatched identifier and a source request against an installation without metadata fail before deletion.
Positive unit check: confirm removal by configured name and by persisted source deletes the intended installed directory.
Isolation check: confirm another installed extension remains after removal.
Side-effect identity check: confirm enablement cleanup, storage selection, and telemetry use the resolved canonical configured name.
Regression check: confirm internal name-based lifecycle callers, including update replacement, remain compatible.
stop_conditions: Stop if installed records do not expose persisted source metadata; do not invent source identity from names or paths.
Stop if source identity is ambiguous across installed records until a disambiguation contract is established.
Stop and fail safely if neither canonical name nor recorded source matches the request.
Stop extraction-level validation claims short of asserting a successful local test run, because only the committed test oracle—not an execution result—was available in this checkout.
unresolved_or_deferred: The committed tests demonstrate exact source-string matching but do not explicitly execute mixed-case name or source inputs, even though the implementation lowercases both operands.
The behavior for duplicate installed records with the same recorded source is unspecified; Array.find would select the first loaded record.
The CLI success message echoes the caller-supplied identifier rather than the resolved canonical name; the change does not establish whether that presentation is intentional.
A local Vitest result is unavailable because the provided checkout's tracked working-tree files were already deleted; validation is grounded in committed test code rather than a fresh execution.

unresolved_questions: Does the product guarantee uniqueness of installMetadata.source across installed extensions, or should source-based removal detect and reject ambiguity?
Should source identifiers receive path or URL canonicalization beyond case folding, such as trailing-slash, .git-suffix, relative-path, or platform-specific path normalization?
Should the command's positional variable be renamed from 'name' to 'identifier' or its success output use the resolved canonical name?
The issue bundle lacks PR body, review discussion, and status-check results, so design rationale and CI execution status cannot be independently established.

title: Detect extension changes and reconcile the live runtime without restarting the session
before: At parent 271664b34b15c55366815ccb11f3eeb0698b8ad5, extension-manager operations could directly refresh MCP tools, skill and subagent caches, and hierarchical memory, but the interactive session had no extension-package filesystem watcher, no shared stale/reload state, no manual package reload command, and no content-only refresh path. Out-of-band edits to installed or linked extension commands, skills, agents, hooks, manifests, context, or package topology therefore were not reconciled into the running session. Configured hooks also had no reload operation that preserved agent-scoped hooks and enabled state.
after: At 151d2694136da5d89c8133bbdb8c08897ae2c107, the CLI watches installed and active linked extension roots, classifies command/skill/agent edits for debounced automatic content refresh and package-level edits for explicit reload, suppresses watcher noise during manager-owned mutations, and coordinates concurrent changes through session-scoped refresh state. A manual reload command rebuilds the extension cache, the multi-component runtime, and slash commands from a coherent snapshot. Core refresh now covers MCP, LSP, skills, subagents, configured hooks, and hierarchical memory with explicit failure propagation, while configured-hook reload preserves agent-scoped hooks and enabled state and rolls back on failure.
diff: The implementation adds ExtensionFileWatcher, ExtensionRefreshState, CLI runtime reload helpers, a manual reload slash command, startup/UI wiring, localized feedback, and tests. It adds native id-paired mutation lifecycle events to the extension manager, expands the core runtime refresh contract to MCP/LSP/hooks, and adds transactional configured-hook reload. The watcher uses conservative path classification, linked-root discovery, bootstrap watching, symlink avoidance, stale-file tracking, generation guards, and mutation suppression. Content refresh is debounced and serialized with a bounded pending-pass loop; package refresh rebuilds cache, runtime components, commands, and a capability summary.

* feat: extension file reload — watch for plugin changes and hot-reload runtime

- Extract refreshExtensionRuntime to centralize MCP, skills, subagents, hooks, and memory refresh
- Add ExtensionFileWatcher (chokidar) for auto-detecting extension file changes
- Add ExtensionRefreshState with per-session scoped instance and mutation suppression
- Replace monkey-patching with ExtensionManager native mutation listeners
- Add /reload-plugins slash command with i18n-aware summary across all 9 locales
- Add auto-refresh of extension content (commands/skills/agents) on file change
- Add HookRegistry.reloadConfiguredHooks() with correct error recovery
- Fix async mutation pairing via id-based Map instead of LIFO stack
- Fix bootstrap watcher close() UB with queueMicrotask deferral
- Fix concurrent refresh with runningRef/pendingRef guard
- Fix error propagation from refreshExtensionContentRuntime to UI
- Fix isIgnored cross-platform path splitting (path.sep → regex)
- Fix wrong ExtensionMutationEvent type via import from core
- Fix addItem on unmounted component with mountedRef guard
- Set followSymlinks: false on chokidar watchers

* fix: address extension reload review feedback

episode.before: At parent 271664b34b15c55366815ccb11f3eeb0698b8ad5, extension-manager operations could directly refresh MCP tools, skill and subagent caches, and hierarchical memory, but the interactive session had no extension-package filesystem watcher, no shared stale/reload state, no manual package reload command, and no content-only refresh path. Out-of-band edits to installed or linked extension commands, skills, agents, hooks, manifests, context, or package topology therefore were not reconciled into the running session. Configured hooks also had no reload operation that preserved agent-scoped hooks and enabled state.
episode.after: At 151d2694136da5d89c8133bbdb8c08897ae2c107, the CLI watches installed and active linked extension roots, classifies command/skill/agent edits for debounced automatic content refresh and package-level edits for explicit reload, suppresses watcher noise during manager-owned mutations, and coordinates concurrent changes through session-scoped refresh state. A manual reload command rebuilds the extension cache, the multi-component runtime, and slash commands from a coherent snapshot. Core refresh now covers MCP, LSP, skills, subagents, configured hooks, and hierarchical memory with explicit failure propagation, while configured-hook reload preserves agent-scoped hooks and enabled state and rolls back on failure.
episode.diff: The implementation adds ExtensionFileWatcher, ExtensionRefreshState, CLI runtime reload helpers, a manual reload slash command, startup/UI wiring, localized feedback, and tests. It adds native id-paired mutation lifecycle events to the extension manager, expands the core runtime refresh contract to MCP/LSP/hooks, and adds transactional configured-hook reload. The watcher uses conservative path classification, linked-root discovery, bootstrap watching, symlink avoidance, stale-file tracking, generation guards, and mutation suppression. Content refresh is debounced and serialized with a bounded pending-pass loop; package refresh rebuilds cache, runtime components, commands, and a capability summary.

evidence_units.source: issue-bundle.json fields issue_number, pinned_ref, resolved_commit, commit_show_stat, and resolution_url; git show --format=fuller 151d2694136da5d89c8133bbdb8c08897ae2c107

evidence_units.claim: The change adds dedicated watcher, refresh-state, runtime-reload, reload-command, and associated test modules, while modifying startup, UI command processing, the extension manager, core runtime refresh, and hook registry/system integration.

The watcher observes the installed-extension directory and active linked sources, avoids following symlinks, ignores initial events, waits for writes to settle, and classifies commands/skills/agents as automatic refresh while manifests and hooks are package-stale.

When the extension directory does not yet exist, a parent bootstrap watcher detects its creation, marks state stale, and defers watcher restart to a microtask; watcher generations reject buffered events from stopped instances.

Shared refresh state deduplicates package-stale notifications, blocks content refresh while package reload is required, records changes arriving during reload, re-emits deferred work after success, and keeps reload-needed state on failure.

Mutation notification suppression is depth-counted, remains active briefly after settlement, supports synchronous and promise-returning operations, and invokes settlement only after overlapping suppressions end.

The extension manager emits native start/end mutation events with unique ids, wraps runtime-relevant mutations in try/finally, and the watcher pairs suppression callbacks by id before restarting its roots after mutations settle.
Content-only refresh refreshes the extension cache, skill cache, subagent cache, and slash commands; independent legs settle before aggregated errors are reported, and safe mode skips the operation.

The slash-command processor debounces content events, serializes refreshes, records a pending pass for changes arriving during execution, stops if package reload becomes necessary, and bounds repeated passes.
Manual package reload rejects safe mode, refreshes the extension cache and full runtime, rebuilds slash commands, and summarizes active extension capabilities.

The manual reload command marks reload start, invokes package reload with command rebuilding, clears state on success, preserves reload-needed state on failure, and returns localized success or error feedback.

Core runtime refresh requires MCP reconciliation first, then reconciles LSP, settles skills/subagents/hooks in parallel, attempts hierarchical-memory refresh, and surfaces hook and LSP failures individually or as an aggregate.
In the parent, core refresh restarted MCP through the tool registry, refreshed only skills and subagents, and attempted hierarchical-memory refresh; it did not reconcile LSP or configured hooks.

Configured-hook reload snapshots prior entries and enabled states, retains agent-scoped entries, rebuilds configured hooks, restores matching enabled states, and restores the entire previous registry if rebuilding throws.
Interactive startup creates one session-scoped refresh state, omits the watcher in bare or safe mode, starts the watcher otherwise, and supplies that shared state to UI consumers.

Watcher tests cover installed and linked roots, path classification, inactive-root exclusion, ignored files, bootstrap watching, mutation-settlement restart, stale-generation rejection, overlapping id pairing, and cleanup of pending suppressions.
Refresh-state tests verify deduplication, mutation suppression, post-mutation windows, changes during reload, stale-over-content priority, failed-reload state, and overlapping suppression settlement.

Runtime helper tests verify full package refresh and capability counts, safe-mode rejection, content refresh of all independent legs, continued settlement before failure reporting, and absent subagent-manager handling.

Core refresh tests verify ordering and coverage, MCP failure propagation, LSP partial and thrown failures, continued independent refresh, delayed hook failure propagation, aggregate failures, and best-effort memory refresh.
Hook tests prove configured reload preserves agent-scoped hooks and enabled state and restores all prior hooks on failure.

UI processor tests prove debounced automatic content refresh, visible failure feedback, suppression while package reload is needed, retry messaging after package reload failure, and cancellation when manual reload starts.

The committed test suite provides direct behavioral oracles for classification, lifecycle coordination, component reconciliation, error propagation, and hook-state preservation; no execution result for these tests is present in the supplied evidence.

candidate_workflows.name: reconcile-live-extension-changes
candidate_workflows.title: Reconcile live extension changes at the narrowest safe scope
candidate_workflows.description: Watch extension-owned files, classify each change, coordinate concurrent lifecycle activity, automatically refresh content-only capabilities, and require a coherent package reload when broader runtime state may have changed.

workflow_graph.goal: Keep a running interactive session consistent with extension files while avoiding unsafe partial application, watcher feedback loops, and loss of session-scoped runtime state.
when_to_use: A long-lived process loads extensible capabilities from files that users or development tools can edit outside the process.
Some extension changes can be refreshed locally, while manifests, hooks, topology, or referenced configuration require a coherent whole-package rebuild.
Programmatic extension mutations and filesystem notifications may overlap or echo one another.
anti_goals: Do not hot-apply arbitrary or unknown extension files.
Do not treat security-sensitive hook edits as content-only refreshes.
Do not change extension discovery, installation-source, marketplace, or conversion semantics as part of reload coordination.
Do not follow extension-provided symlinks into arbitrary external paths.
Do not hide MCP, LSP, hook, or aggregated content-refresh failures behind a success message.
not_applicable_when: The process has no persistent runtime state or always restarts after extension changes.
The session is in bare or safe mode where extensions or reload are disabled.
All extension changes are already performed through one transactional owner and no out-of-band filesystem edits are supported.
The host cannot identify semantic file classes or provide subsystem refresh APIs with validation oracles.
inputs: Active extension metadata and roots, including linked sources
Filesystem event kind and absolute changed path
Session-scoped refresh state and event channel
Extension-manager mutation lifecycle events
Runtime subsystem refresh interfaces
Slash-command rebuild callback
Safe-mode and bare-mode status
workflow_graph.entry_state: The running session may hold extension cache, commands, skills, agents, hooks, external servers, and context that no longer match files on disk, or a manager-owned mutation may be writing those files.
workflow_graph.exit_state: Every observed relevant change is either applied through a completed bounded content refresh or represented by a visible package-reload requirement; after successful package reload, runtime components and commands reflect one refreshed extension snapshot, while concurrent or failed changes remain retryable.

steps.condition: A filesystem event occurs under an installed root, an active linked source, or a tracked referenced file.
steps.validation: The event resolves to automatic content refresh, package-stale, or ignored using tests for each supported path class.

steps.condition: Always for admitted automatic or package-stale events, and around manager-owned mutations and manual reloads.
steps.validation: State tests show deduplication, priority, deferred-event retention, overlap-safe suppression, and retry state after failure.

steps.condition: The change is limited to commands, skills, or agents; safe mode is off; no package-stale flag exists.
steps.validation: All content cache and command legs settle, another bounded pass runs for concurrent changes, and any errors are aggregated and shown.

steps.condition: A package reload reaches the configured-hook refresh leg.
steps.validation: Agent-scoped hooks and enabled states survive successful reload, and the prior complete registry survives failure.

steps.condition: The change affects package topology, manifests, hooks, context, enablement, install metadata, or referenced runtime configuration, or automatic content refresh reports failure and the user retries with package reload.
steps.validation: Cache, runtime subsystems, and commands are rebuilt; material partial failures are returned; success reports active capability counts and clears stale state.

validation_ladder: Unit-test path classification for installed roots, linked roots, tracked referenced files, ignored files, topology creation/removal, and missing manifests.
Unit-test refresh state for deduplication, overlapping mutation suppression, changes during reload, stale-over-content priority, and failure retryability.
Unit-test content refresh for cache and command coverage, independent-leg settlement, aggregated errors, safe-mode behavior, debounce, and cancellation.
Unit-test configured-hook reload for session-hook preservation, enabled-state preservation, and transactional rollback.
Unit-test package runtime reconciliation for MCP-first behavior, LSP and hook failure propagation, best-effort legs, command rebuilding, and summary counts.

Exercise the interactive session by editing each supported file class and confirming either immediate capability visibility or a package-reload prompt, followed by successful reload or actionable failure feedback.
stop_conditions: Stop automatic refresh when the session enters safe or bare mode.
Stop content-only reconciliation and require package reload when package-stale state is set.
Stop classifying unknown files as reloadable unless a semantic owner and validation oracle are added.
Stop and retain retry-needed state when a material package reload leg fails.
Stop repeated automatic passes at the configured bound and surface the noisy-change failure.
unresolved_or_deferred: No test execution or CI result was supplied or run for this extraction; validation evidence is the committed test code and its asserted oracles.
Per-extension incremental external-server restart remains intentionally deferred; the implementation uses existing global reconciliation entry points.
Unknown extension files remain ignored until explicitly assigned a safe lifecycle class.
The extraction does not establish behavior outside the interactive CLI startup path.

unresolved_questions: Whether all committed tests passed in CI is not established by the checkout or supplied bundle.
The exact downstream recovery behavior after partial MCP or LSP reconciliation depends on subsystem implementations outside this bounded episode.
No cross-repository peer workflows or untouched holdout result were supplied, so this episode supports Actions and an issue Workflow only, not promotion of a universal Resolution Pattern.

title: Close active terminal hyperlinks at truncation boundaries
before: At parent commit 6bfd50261dfa103a761c2638965248381251827c, terminal text truncation finalized a retained prefix by appending only an SGR reset and optional ellipsis. If the prefix contained an OSC 8 hyperlink opener but truncation omitted its later closer, the emitted string left the hyperlink active beyond the retained label.
after: At commit b780d20aa17c4144ace7bff728150993236b88ee, truncation scans the retained prefix for OSC 8 state. When a hyperlink remains active, it emits an OSC 8 close using the opener's BEL or ST terminator before the existing SGR reset and ellipsis. A focused test asserts the exact BEL-terminated output.
diff: The change adds getActiveOsc8Close(), which reuses terminal-sequence extraction, OSC 8 parsing, and close formatting to derive a matching close sequence from the retained prefix. finalizeTruncatedResult() now inserts that close before its reset in both ellipsis and no-ellipsis branches. The regression test constructs a BEL-terminated link whose label is truncated and verifies that the synthesized close precedes the reset and ellipsis.

commit.subject: fix(tui): close truncated OSC 8 links (#7657)
commit.body_excerpt:
When truncateToWidth() cut through an OSC 8 hyperlink label, the retained prefix could leave the hyperlink open. Close an active hyperlink before the existing reset and ellipsis, preserving its BEL or ST terminator.
Added a focused regression test for the reported BEL-terminated case.
